name: Chera kingdom
summary: The Cheras were one of the three crowned dynasties of the ancient Tamil country, ruling the Kerala coast and the Kongu interior from Vanchi-Karur and growing rich on the pepper that Roman and Arab ships bought at Muziris. Their power faded after the 3rd century, but a medieval Chera kingdom, the Perumals of Mahodayapuram (Kodungallur), arose c. 844 and ruled central Kerala for almost three centuries. Chola invasions from c. 988 forced it into submission, and in the early 12th century it dissolved into local kingdoms such as Venad.

events.text: c. 260 BCE: Ashoka's edicts name the Cheras as free neighbours of his empire
events.detail: The Cheras are among the earliest South Indian powers named in writing. The rock edicts of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka, carved in the mid-3rd century BCE, list the peoples beyond his frontiers, among them the Cholas, the Pandyas and the 'Kedalaputo', the Cheras. They lay outside his empire and are treated as friendly neighbours. Historians usually date the Chera state from this time, although some argue that in these early centuries the Cheras were a group of chiefdoms rather than a fully formed kingdom, with branches ruling from the Kerala coast and from Karur inland.

events.text: c. 50: Roman, Greek and Arab ships buy Chera pepper at the port of Muziris
events.detail: The Chera coast grew black pepper and other spices that the Roman world prized. In the 1st century CE the Greek sailing guide known as the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea described Muziris, near the mouth of the Periyar river, as a port frequented by Roman, Arab and Greek ships, and Pliny the Elder also wrote about the Cheras. Spices were exchanged for Roman gold, and Roman coins and amphorae have been found at the Chera capital Karur and at Pattanam on the coast. The Cheras even counter-struck Roman silver coins with their own marks.

events.text: c. 150: Pugalur inscriptions near Karur name three generations of Chera kings
events.detail: Two nearly identical Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions in a rock shelter at Pugalur, near Karur, dated to about the 2nd century CE, are among the best evidence for the early Chera kings. They record a rock shelter made for a Jain monk named Chenkayapan and name three generations of rulers: Athan Cheral Irumporai, Perum Kadungon and Ilam Kadungo. They confirm that kings of the Irumporai branch ruled from Karur, in the Kongu country, while a western branch held the coast around Muziris. The two branches probably competed for leadership of the Chera realm.

events.text: c. 180: Senguttuvan, the most celebrated early Chera king, reigns
events.detail: Senguttuvan, called 'Kadal Pirakottiya', is the most celebrated of the early Chera kings praised in the Sangam anthology Pathitruppathu, and he appears in the Tamil epic Silappathikaram. The epic links him to the Sri Lankan king Gajabahu, and this synchronism is the main reason historians date him and his line to the 2nd century CE, though the method rests on guesswork. Other kings of the same age are credited in the poems with conquering the Kongu country and defeating combined Pandya and Chola armies, although praise poetry of this kind is hard to verify.

events.text: c. 215: The Chera king Mantharam Cheral is captured by the Pandya Nedunjeliyan II
events.detail: Wars among the three crowned Tamil kings were frequent. In the early 3rd century, by the usual reconstruction of the Sangam rulers, the Chera king Mantharam Cheral Irumporai, who governed a large territory, was captured by the Pandya king Nedunjeliyan II, although he later escaped. Nedunjeliyan is remembered for a victory at Talaiyalanganam over the forces of the Chera and Chola kings. Such defeats weakened the Irumporai Cheras of Karur at the very end of the Sangam age, after which Chera power went into a long decline.

events.text: c. 300: Chera power fades as the Kalabhras overrun the Tamil country
events.detail: Between the 3rd and 5th centuries the power of the early Cheras declined sharply, and the history of their lands becomes poorly documented. The Cheras of Karur, sometimes called the Keralas, seem to have kept a hold on part of the former Chera territory. Across the Tamil country the Kalabhras displaced the old royal houses, and later the region fell under the domination of the Chalukyas, Pallavas and Pandyas, then the Rashtrakutas and Cholas. For more than five centuries no strong Chera kingdom is recorded on the Kerala coast.

events.text: c. 844: Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara rules a new Chera kingdom from Mahodayapuram
events.detail: In the 8th or 9th century central Kerala separated from the older Chera realm in the Kongu country and formed a new kingdom whose kings were called Perumals. Its capital was Mahodayapuram, also called Makotai, at modern Kodungallur near the ancient port of Muziris. The earliest known king, Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara, began to reign around 844. He was allied with the Chola king Aditya I and is credited with helping the Cholas win the western Tamil country in the late 9th century. The new kings claimed descent from the ancient Cheras.

events.text: c. 849: The Quilon copper plates grant land to a Christian church at Kollam
events.detail: In about 849, the fifth year of Sthanu Ravi, Ayyan Adikal, the chieftain of Venad in the far south, issued a grant to the Christian merchant Mar Sapir Iso for the Tarisappalli church at Kollam (Quilon). It gave land and bonded workers to the church and made two merchant guilds, the Anjuvannam and the Manigramam, tenants of the settlement, with tax privileges. Witnesses signed in Arabic, Middle Persian and Judeo-Persian. It is the oldest surviving inscription of the medieval Chera kingdom and shows Christian, Jewish and Muslim traders at work on its coast.

events.text: c. 988: The Chola king Rajaraja I wins a victory at Kandalur Salai
events.detail: For over a century the Perumals were allies of the Cholas, and King Vijayaraga married his daughters to the Chola king Parantaka I. That changed under Rajaraja I, perhaps because the Cholas wanted to break the Chera hold on the pepper trade. His earliest inscriptions celebrate a triumph at Kandalur Salai, near modern Thiruvananthapuram, around 988, and his general captured the port of Vizhinjam. Chola inscriptions appear in Kanyakumari district in the 990s and in the Thiruvananthapuram area by the early 1000s, as the southern Chera lands slipped from Perumal control.

events.text: c. 1000: Bhaskara Ravi grants trading rights to the Jewish merchant Joseph Rabban
events.detail: Bhaskara Ravi, who ruled from about 962 to 1021, issued a copper-plate charter at Muyirikode, near his capital, to Joseph Rabban, a Jewish merchant magnate of Kodungallur. It gave Rabban the rights of the Anjuvannam merchant guild, including toll and customs privileges, and made them hereditary for his descendants. Historians date it to about 1000. Some think the grant rewarded Jewish merchants for financial or military help to the Chera state at a time of Chola threats. Cochin's Jewish community long treasured the plates as the deed of their settlement.

events.text: c. 1005: Chola armies defeat the rulers of Kollam and Kodungallur
events.detail: Chola pressure turned into conquest. A Chola inscription at Senur dated 1005 boasts of the destruction of the Pandya capital, Madurai, and the defeat of the rulers of Kollam, Kolla-desham and Kodungallur, the Chera capital. The Chola subjugation of Kerala is dated to the early years of the 11th century. Under Rajaraja's son Rajendra I, Chola control over Kerala became firm, and the land was held for a time as an appanage for junior Chola princes. The Perumal kings survived, but as subordinates of the Cholas.

events.text: c. 1102: Rama Kulasekhara retakes Kollam and holds a royal council there
events.detail: The Chola king Kulottunga I brought the Chera and Pandya lands back under Chola control in campaigns of 1077 to 1081, and Chola forces pushed north to Kollam around 1097. The last Perumal, Rama Kulasekhara, crowned around 1089, reportedly retook the city around 1102 and used it as a second headquarters. An inscription at the Rameswaram temple in Kollam, dated 1102, records a council at which the king publicly atoned for wrongs against Brahmins, an unusual act for a ruling Chera. Chola campaigns in south Kerala continued until about 1118.

events.text: c. 1122: The last Perumal's reign ends and Kerala splits into local kingdoms
events.detail: A Chola inscription from Thanjavur dated 1122 mentions 'the flight of the Chera king to the sea'. Rama Kulasekhara's reign ended in the early 1120s, and with it the medieval Chera kingdom dissolved into several local powers; historians see changing land relations as a key cause, as local Nair leaders took over the running of temples. Tradition holds that his son Vira Kerala became the first independent ruler of Venad in the south, while the rulers of Kozhikode and Kochi rose elsewhere. A popular legend says the last Cheraman Perumal divided his kingdom and left for Mecca.

name: Pandya dynasty
summary: The Pandyas of Madurai were the longest-lived of the three crowned Tamil dynasties, known to Ashoka and to Roman writers for the pearls traded through their port at Korkai. Displaced by the Kalabhras, they revived under Kadungon c. 590 and fought the Pallavas for the south until the Cholas took Madurai in 910. Rising again in 1216, they overthrew the Cholas and under Jatavarman Sundara Pandya ruled from Sri Lanka to Nellore, until civil war and invasions from the Delhi Sultanate in 1311–1323 ended their empire.

events.text: c. 260 BCE: Ashoka's edicts list the Pandyas as friendly neighbours
events.detail: The Pandya kingdom, centred on Madurai in the far south of the Tamil country, already existed by the 4th century BCE: the Greek envoy Megasthenes described a Pandya queen whose realm had 365 villages, each supplying the palace for one day. In the mid-3rd century BCE the rock edicts of the Mauryan emperor Ashoka named the Pandyas, with the Cholas and Cheras, among the friendly peoples beyond his frontier. The Mauryas never conquered the far south, and the Pandyas kept their independence.

events.text: c. 13 CE: A Pandya embassy reaches the Roman emperor Augustus
events.detail: The Pandyas grew rich from the pearl fisheries of their coast, traded through Korkai and Alagankulam, and from commerce with the Mediterranean. According to Nicolaus of Damascus, as reported by the geographer Strabo, an ambassador sent by a king called Pandion met the Roman emperor Augustus around 13 CE. In the 1st century CE Pliny and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea described the Pandya kingdom, and around 140 the geographer Ptolemy recorded Madurai as the royal seat of Pandion. Earlier, the Kalinga king Kharavela had boasted of taking Pandya pearls.

events.text: c. 215: Nedunjeliyan II defeats the Chera and Chola kings at Talaiyalanganam
events.detail: The Sangam poems of the early centuries CE describe Madurai as a great city and the traditional home of the Tamil literary academies. Their most famous Pandya hero is Nedunjeliyan II, who won a battle at Talaiyalanganam against the combined forces of the Chera and Chola kings and their allies. The Chera king Mantharam Cheral Irumporai was captured, though he later escaped. Dating the Sangam rulers is difficult, and the victory can be placed only roughly, in the late 2nd or early 3rd century, near the end of the early Pandya kingdom.

events.text: c. 250: The Kalabhras displace the early Pandya kingdom
events.detail: From around the middle of the 3rd century the Kalabhras, a dynasty whose origins remain obscure, displaced the early Pandyas and the other old Tamil royal houses. Their rule lasted until the late 6th century and is poorly documented; later Pandya inscriptions looked back on it as a time of darkness. Little is known of the Pandyas themselves for more than three centuries, although an embassy from them is recorded at the court of the Roman emperor Julian around 361. Madurai would not again be the seat of a strong Pandya king until the 590s.

events.text: c. 590: Kadungon drives out the Kalabhras and revives the Pandya kingdom
events.detail: Late in the 6th century the Kalabhras were overthrown. In the north the Pallava king Simhavishnu struck at them, and in the south Kadungon, who took the title Pandyadhiraja, restored Pandya rule with Madurai as his capital. The later Velvikudi inscription calls him a resplendent sun rising from the dark clouds of the Kalabhras and says he destroyed the cities of his foes. Most historians date his reign to about 590–620, though some prefer c. 560–590. The Tamil country was now divided between the Pallavas of Kanchi in the north and the Pandyas in the south.

events.text: c. 840: Srimara Srivallabha invades Sri Lanka and plunders Anuradhapura
events.detail: The revived Pandyas expanded through the 7th and 8th centuries; Jatila Parantaka Nedunjadaiyan (c. 765–815) conquered the Kongu country and Venad. His son Srimara Srivallabha (c. 815–862) took the war overseas. During the reign of Sena I of Anuradhapura he launched a seaborne invasion of Sri Lanka; his forces occupied and plundered the capital, Anuradhapura, and he withdrew after making peace with the exiled king. The exact year is uncertain. At home Srimara fought the Pallavas, losing to Nandivarman III's coalition at Tellaru but winning at Kudamukku (Kumbakonam) around 859.

events.text: c. 862: A Sri Lankan army helps Varaguna II seize the Pandya throne
events.detail: Sri Lanka took its revenge. King Sena II allied with a rival Pandya prince, Varaguna II, also called Maya Pandya, and sent an army to the mainland. According to the sources his forces marched on Madurai, though they failed to sack it, and placed Varaguna on the throne; some records say Srimara died of wounds soon after the fighting. Varaguna II became king around 862. The Pandya adventure in Sri Lanka had rebounded on the kingdom, and Varaguna's reign would end in a heavy defeat by a coalition from the north.

events.text: c. 879: The Pandyas are defeated at Thirupurambiyam near Kumbakonam
events.detail: Varaguna II tried to restore Pandya power in the north of the Tamil country. Around 879 he met a coalition of the Pallava prince Aparajita, the Western Ganga king Prithvipati I and the Chola Aditya I at Thirupurambiyam, near Kumbakonam; sources date the battle between about 879 and 885. The allies won, although Prithvipati was killed and the victory was costly. The Pandyas were badly weakened and Varaguna retired. The battle is seen as a turning point: it opened the way for the Cholas, who soon overwhelmed both the Pallavas and the Pandyas.

events.text: 910: The Chola Parantaka I takes Madurai; Rajasimha II flees to Sri Lanka
events.detail: After Thirupurambiyam the Cholas grew quickly. Aditya I annexed the Pallava kingdom, and his son Parantaka I turned south against the Pandyas. In 910 he captured Madurai, and the Pandya king Maravarman Rajasimha II fled to Sri Lanka. For about three centuries afterwards the Pandyas survived only as subordinate or rebel princes. Rajaraja I took Madurai again in the late 10th or early 11th century, Rajendra I governed the south through 'Chola Pandya' viceroys, and Kulottunga I's reign opened with a Pandya revolt that he had to put down.

events.text: 1216: Maravarman Sundara Pandya I sacks Thanjavur and Uraiyur
events.detail: By the late 12th century Chola power was fading, and the Pandyas, after a civil war of 1169–1177, recovered. Maravarman Sundara Pandya I, who became king in 1216, laid the foundation of a new Pandya supremacy. He invaded the Chola country, sacked Uraiyur and Thanjavur and drove King Kulottunga III into exile; Kulottunga later submitted and accepted Pandya overlordship. The Hoysalas of Karnataka stepped in to protect the Cholas, and at Mahendramangalam on the Kaveri a Hoysala-backed Chola army defeated the Pandyas, but the balance of power in the Tamil country had shifted south.

events.text: 1258: Jatavarman Sundara Pandya takes Kanchipuram and intervenes in Sri Lanka
events.detail: Jatavarman Sundara Pandya I, crowned at Chidambaram in 1251, was the greatest Pandya conqueror. He forced the Chola king Rajendra III to accept his overlordship, seized the Hoysala southern capital at Kannanur Koppam near Srirangam and confined the Hoysalas to the Mysore plateau. In 1258 his forces killed the Telugu Chola ruler Vijaya Gandagopala and took Kanchipuram, and the same year he intervened in Sri Lanka. He also defeated a Kakatiya-led army at Mudugur. By his death in 1268 Pandya power reached Nellore and Kadapa, and he gilded the roofs of the Chidambaram and Srirangam temples.

events.text: c. 1279: Kulasekara I defeats the Hoysalas and Cholas; the Chola line ends
events.detail: Maravarman Kulasekara I (1268–1310) completed Pandya supremacy. Around 1279 he defeated the combined forces of the Hoysala king Ramanatha and the Chola king Rajendra III, the last of his line, and afterwards the Pandyas faced no serious rival in the Tamil country. Kulasekara invaded Sri Lanka and carried the sacred Tooth Relic back to the Pandya country, and the island stayed under Pandya control until about 1308. The Venetian traveller Marco Polo, who visited in 1288 and 1293, described the kingdom and the very fine pearls found there.

events.text: 1311: Malik Kafur's army raids the Pandya country during a civil war
events.detail: When Kulasekara I died in 1310, his sons Vira Pandya and Sundara Pandya fought over the throne. The quarrel opened the way for the Delhi Sultanate, whose armies were already raiding the Deccan. In March 1311 a Khalji army under Malik Kafur marched into Pandya territory; the brothers fled, and the invaders chased them without success before returning to Delhi by late April with their plunder. The Pandyas lost south Kerala by 1312. Sundara Pandya even sought Khalji help against his brother, and another Sultanate expedition followed in 1314.

events.text: 1323: A Tughluq army invades; the Pandya lands become the province of Ma'bar
events.detail: In 1323 a new Sultanate expedition led by Jauna Khan, also called Ulugh Khan and later Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq, invaded the south for his father Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq. Ulugh Khan annexed the former Pandya kingdom as the province of Ma'bar, and in the same year the Jaffna kingdom in Sri Lanka threw off Pandya influence. Around 1334 the governor Jalal ud-Din Hasan Khan declared independence and founded the Madurai Sultanate. The Pandyas survived as minor rulers based at Tenkasi until the late 16th century, but their empire was gone.

name: Satavahana dynasty
summary: The Satavahanas, called Andhras in the Puranas, rose in the Deccan in the 2nd century BCE (an older reckoning places their start in the 3rd), ruling from Pratishthana (Paithan) and later also from Amaravati in the east. Satakarni I pushed into Malwa and Vidarbha, but the western Deccan was lost to the Shaka satraps until Gautamiputra Satakarni won it back, beginning a long contest between the two powers. After a last revival under Yajna Sri Satakarni, the realm broke up c. 224 CE among the Abhiras, Ikshvakus, Chutus and Pallavas.

events.text: c. 110 BCE: Simuka, the founding king, is in his 16th year (Kanaganahalli)
events.detail: The Satavahanas were a Deccan family whose homeland is still argued over: some scholars place it in Andhra, others around Pratishthana in Maharashtra or in northern Karnataka. The Puranas say the founder, Simuka, overthrew the last Kanva rulers and reigned for 23 years. An inscription at the Buddhist stupa of Kanaganahalli, on the Bhima river, mentions year 16 of Simuka and is dated to about 110 BCE. Most modern historians use evidence like this to start the dynasty in the late 2nd century BCE, though an older 'long chronology' pushes it back to the 3rd century BCE.

events.text: c. 100 BCE: Kanha extends Satavahana rule west to Nashik
events.detail: Simuka was followed by his brother Kanha (Krishna). He carried Satavahana rule westward to Nashik, on the upper Godavari, a town on the routes between the Deccan plateau and the ports of the Konkan coast. An inscription in Cave 19 of the Pandavleni caves near Nashik dates to his reign and is one of the earliest records of the dynasty. Holding Nashik gave the Satavahanas a foothold in the western Deccan, the region they would fight over with rival powers for the next three centuries.

events.text: c. 70 BCE: Satakarni I conquers Malwa and Vidarbha and performs horse sacrifices
events.detail: Satakarni I, the third king, was the first great conqueror of the line. Taking advantage of turmoil among the Indo-Greeks and other northern powers, he seized western Malwa, Anupa in the Narmada valley and Vidarbha in the east. His widow Nayanika later recorded his reign in an inscription in the Naneghat pass, on the trade route from Junnar down to the coast, listing the costly Vedic rites he performed, including the Ashvamedha horse sacrifice and the Rajasuya, both claims to supreme kingship. The Kalinga king Kharavela also names him, though scholars disagree over whether the two ever fought.

events.text: c. 50 BCE: Satakarni II takes eastern Malwa from the Shungas
events.detail: His successor, usually identified as Satakarni II, is said to have reigned for 56 years. He captured eastern Malwa from the declining Shunga dynasty, carrying Satavahana power north of the Narmada into central India. An inscription on the southern gateway of the great Buddhist stupa at Sanchi records a gift made under a 'King Satakarni', most probably this king, and is dated to between about 50 BCE and the turn of the era. The Satavahanas now held a wide belt of land across the northern and western Deccan.

events.text: c. 78: Gautamiputra Satakarni defeats the Shaka satrap Nahapana
events.detail: In the 1st century CE the Western Kshatrapas, Shaka rulers of Gujarat and Malwa, took the Satavahanas' western lands, and their king Nahapana ruled around Nashik and Pune through his son-in-law Rishabhadatta. Gautamiputra Satakarni struck back and defeated him. In the Jogalthembi hoard, found in Nashik district, many of Nahapana's silver coins were restruck with Gautamiputra's name. The date is disputed: some scholars place the victory in 78 CE, others around 124 CE, and his reign is dated anywhere from c. 60–85 to c. 106–130. Either way, the western Deccan returned to Satavahana rule.

events.text: c. 100: Queen mother Gautami Balashri's Nashik inscription lauds Gautamiputra's realm
events.detail: Gautamiputra's son Vasishthiputra Pulumavi kept his father's lands and added the Bellary region in the south. In Pulumavi's 19th regnal year, Gautamiputra's mother, Gautami Balashri, dedicated Cave 3 at the Pandavleni caves near Nashik to Buddhist monks, with a long inscription praising her son. It claims Gautamiputra ruled from Malwa and Saurashtra to the Krishna river and from the Konkan to Vidarbha, that he destroyed the Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas, and that his horses drank from three oceans. Historians treat the boast with caution; his hold on the far north-west was probably short-lived.

events.text: c. 150: The satrap Rudradaman twice defeats Satakarni, lord of Dakshinapatha
events.detail: The Western Kshatrapas recovered under Rudradaman I, who ruled c. 130–150. His Sanskrit inscription on a rock at Junagadh in Gujarat, dated 150 CE, boasts that he twice defeated Satakarni, 'lord of Dakshinapatha' (the Deccan), in fair fight but spared him because they were closely related: Rudradaman had given a daughter in marriage to a Satavahana prince. Which Satakarni he meant is still argued over. Rudradaman won back most of Nahapana's old lands except the area around Pune and Nashik, and the Satavahanas were pushed back onto the Deccan and their eastern lands around Amaravati.

events.text: c. 170: Yajna Sri Satakarni revives the dynasty from the Konkan to Andhra
events.detail: Yajna Sri Satakarni, who reigned from roughly the 170s to the 190s, was the last strong king of the main line. He won back territory from the Western Kshatrapas and issued silver coins copying theirs, a sign that he now controlled lands where satrap money had circulated. His inscriptions at Nashik and Kanheri in the west and in the Guntur region in the east show him ruling across the whole Deccan from sea to sea. Some of his coins carry the image of a ship, pointing to the importance of seaborne trade.

events.text: c. 190: The Abhiras seize the Nashik region in the north-west
events.detail: Yajna Sri's revival did not last. Late in his reign the Abhiras captured the northern parts of the Satavahana realm around Nashik. The loss cut the dynasty off from the western routes and ports that had brought it so much wealth. After Yajna Sri, a series of short-lived kings, including Madhariputra Isvarasena, Vijaya and Vasishthiputra Chadha Satakarni, ruled a shrinking kingdom whose centre moved steadily east, towards the lower Krishna valley in Andhra. Nashik, once the heart of Satavahana power in the west, would not be recovered.

events.text: c. 217: Pulumavi IV, last king of the main line, comes to the throne
events.detail: Pulumavi IV is counted as the last king of the main Satavahana line, reigning from about 217 to about 224. His power was concentrated in the eastern Deccan, in the lower Krishna valley. The region was rich, and during his reign Buddhist monuments were being built at Nagarjunakonda and Amaravati, among the great Buddhist centres of ancient India. But royal authority over the outlying provinces had weakened, and local families who had governed in the name of the Satavahanas were ready to rule in their own right.

events.text: Satavahana rule ends; successor dynasties divide the Deccan
events.detail: Around 224–225 the Satavahana state broke apart. Its western part around Nashik went to the Abhiras, the Krishna–Guntur region in the east to the Andhra Ikshvakus, and northern Karnataka to the Chutus of Banavasi, while the Pallavas rose in the south-east around Kanchi. A collateral Satavahana branch survived in the north until the early 4th century. The Western Kshatrapas, the Satavahanas' old rivals in the west, outlived them by about two centuries, until the Gupta Empire brought their rule to an end.

name: Vakataka dynasty
summary: The Vakatakas rose in the Vidarbha region of the northern Deccan around 250 under Vindhyashakti, and his son Pravarasena I, the only Vakataka to call himself samrat (emperor), spread their rule widely. After him the family split into a main line at Nandivardhana and Pravarapura and a cadet line at Vatsagulma; a marriage to the Guptas around 380–390 drew the main line into the Gupta orbit. Harishena of Vatsagulma, patron of the Ajanta caves, was the last great king, and Vakataka rule faded out in the early 6th century.

events.text: c. 250: Vindhyashakti founds the Vakataka line in the northern Deccan
events.detail: In the 3rd century the Deccan was divided among regional kingdoms. One of them was founded around 250 by Vindhyashakti, a chief named after Vindhyavasini, a goddess of the Vindhya hills. Very little is known about him: later records call him the 'banner of the Vakataka family', and Puranic tradition links him to Vidisha. He ruled until about 275. His family came to control Vidarbha, in what is now eastern Maharashtra, and would become the leading power of the northern Deccan for more than two centuries.

events.text: c. 275: Pravarasena I, the only Vakataka 'samrat', begins a long reign
events.detail: Vindhyashakti's son Pravarasena I ruled for some sixty years, from about 275 to 335. He was the only Vakataka king to take the imperial title samrat, and he performed many grand Vedic sacrifices that advertised his power. His rule is said to have stretched across much of central India and the northern Deccan, making the Vakatakas one of the strongest dynasties of their time. His eldest son Gautamiputra died before him, so the succession passed to a grandson, and the family's unity did not outlast him.

events.text: c. 335: The family splits into the Nandivardhana and Vatsagulma branches
events.detail: On Pravarasena I's death around 335 the kingdom was divided among his descendants. Two branches are known. The main line, under his grandson Rudrasena I, ruled from Nandivardhana (Nagardhan, near Nagpur) in eastern Vidarbha. A younger son, Sarvasena, founded a separate line with its capital at Vatsagulma (Washim) in the west, and is credited with a lost Prakrit poem, the Harivijaya. The two branches lived side by side for about 150 years, each with its own kings, until Harishena of Vatsagulma reunited them late in the 5th century.

events.text: c. 350: A 'Rudradeva' on Samudragupta's pillar may be Rudrasena I
events.detail: To the north, the Gupta king Samudragupta was building an empire across the Ganges plain. His inscription on the Allahabad pillar lists the kings he overthrew, among them a 'Rudradeva'. Some historians identify him with the Vakataka king Rudrasena I, who ruled from Nandivardhana from about 335 to 360; others reject the link, and the question is unsettled. Either way, the Gupta empire now bordered the Vakataka lands, and relations with the Guptas would shape the main Vakataka branch for the next century.

events.text: c. 385: Rudrasena II, husband of a Gupta princess, takes the throne
events.detail: Rather than fight the Guptas, the Vakatakas made an alliance with them. Rudrasena II, king of the main branch from about 385, married Prabhavatigupta, a daughter of the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II and his queen Kuberanaga. The match gave Chandragupta a friendly ally on the southern flank of his empire and tied the two royal houses closely together. Rudrasena II died after a reign of only about five years, leaving three young sons and a widow whose family ruled northern India.

events.text: c. 390–410: Queen Prabhavatigupta rules as regent for her sons
events.detail: When Rudrasena II died around 390, none of his sons was an adult, so Prabhavatigupta governed as regent in the name of the eldest, Divakarasena. She ruled for about twenty years; one of her land grants, found at Pune, is dated in her thirteenth year. She seems to have kept power even after her son came of age. Gupta influence over the Vakatakas peaked in these years, and some historians describe the kingdom as practically part of the Gupta empire, though the evidence for direct Gupta control is thin.

events.text: c. 420: Pravarasena II founds a new capital at Pravarapura
events.detail: Prabhavatigupta's son Pravarasena II ruled the main branch from about 420 to 455. He is the best-documented Vakataka king, known from seventeen copper-plate land grants. He moved the capital from Nandivardhana to a new city, Pravarapura, at Paunar near Wardha, where he built a temple to Rama. He is also credited with the Setubandha, a celebrated poem in Maharashtri Prakrit about Rama's bridge to Lanka. His long and settled reign marked the cultural high point of the eastern Vakataka kingdom.

events.text: c. 455: Narendrasena extends Vakataka influence into central India
events.detail: Pravarasena II was followed by his son Narendrasena, who ruled from about 455 (some accounts say 440) to 480. The close Gupta tie of his grandmother's time had loosened, and the Vakatakas acted as a power in their own right. Vakataka influence spread northward into central India. But the main branch was soon under pressure: Narendrasena's son Prithivishena II, the last known king of this line, was defeated by the Vishnukundina king Madhava Varma II from the eastern Deccan.

events.text: c. 480: Harishena reunites the Vakataka lands; Ajanta's caves flourish
events.detail: Harishena of the Vatsagulma branch was the last great Vakataka king. He probably annexed the weakened main branch, and an inscription in Ajanta Cave XVI credits him with conquests from Gujarat and Malwa to Kalinga and Andhra. He and his courtiers, such as the minister Varahadeva and the vassal Upendragupta, sponsored the magnificent Buddhist caves and paintings at Ajanta. His dates are disputed: the dynasty's genealogy places him c. 475–510, while the art historian Walter Spink dates his reign 460–477 and most of the Ajanta work to c. 460–480.

events.text: c. 500–510: Vakataka rule fades; Kadambas and Kalachuris move in
events.detail: Harishena was followed by two kings whose names are not known, and the end of the dynasty is obscure. One view holds that the Kalachuris of Mahishmati overthrew them. A later Sanskrit tale, the Dashakumaracharita, describes a pleasure-loving last king killed fighting an invasion led by the Kadambas near the Wardha river. A Kadamba record of 519 suggests the Kadambas had annexed the region after about 500. By then the Vakataka kingdom had disappeared, and within a few decades the Chalukyas of Badami would rise as the new power of the Deccan.

name: Pallava dynasty
summary: The Pallavas ruled from Kanchipuram from the late 3rd century, first issuing grants in Prakrit and surviving a raid by the Gupta emperor Samudragupta and the Kalabhra upheaval. Revived by Simhavishnu in the later 6th century, they fought the Chalukyas of Vatapi for more than a century, sacking Vatapi in 642 and building the temples of Mamallapuram and Kanchi. Pressed by the Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas and Pandyas, they finally lost their kingdom when the Chola Aditya I killed the last king, Aparajita, in 897.

events.text: 283: Sivaskandavarman issues Prakrit land grants from Kanchipuram
events.detail: The origins of the Pallavas are debated: they may have begun as feudatories of the Satavahanas, as a local family of the Kanchi region, or as a people of pastoral descent. Their earliest records are three copper-plate grants in Prakrit issued from Kanchipuram by King Sivaskandavarman. One, the Hirahadagalli plates, is dated to 283 CE, in his eighth regnal year. These grants show a dynasty already established at Kanchipuram, a city that would remain the Pallava capital for more than six centuries.

events.text: c. 350: Samudragupta captures and then releases Vishnugopa of Kanchi
events.detail: In the 4th century the Gupta emperor Samudragupta (c. 335–375) led a campaign into the Deccan and the south. His Allahabad Pillar inscription lists Vishnugopa of Kanchi, probably a Pallava regent ruling for his nephew, among twelve southern kings he captured and then released as an act of favour. Most scholars think these kings were restored as tributaries, but some argue that Samudragupta never got beyond the Krishna river and that the boast covers a retreat. Either way, the Pallavas kept their kingdom, and the southern kings were never under direct Gupta rule.

events.text: c. 575: Simhavishnu breaks the Kalabhras and restores Pallava power
events.detail: In the 5th and 6th centuries the Pallavas lost ground: the Vishnukundins took lands in the north, and in the 6th century the Kalabhra invasions threw the Tamil country into upheaval. Late in the 6th century Simhavishnu, whose dates are disputed but are often given as c. 575–600, struck at the Kalabhras and restored Pallava power around Kanchi. The Pandya king Kadungon did the same in the south, and the Tamil country was divided between the Pallavas in the north and the Pandyas around Madurai. His revival began the age of the great Pallava kings.

events.text: c. 600: Mahendravarman I begins Pallava rock-cut temples amid Chalukya wars
events.detail: Simhavishnu's son Mahendravarman I (c. 600–630) expanded the kingdom, but his reign also opened a long struggle with the Chalukyas of Vatapi in the Deccan, whose king Pulakeshin II invaded the Pallava north. Mahendravarman is remembered above all as a patron of the arts. He began the Pallava tradition of temples cut into solid rock, and he is credited with writing the Sanskrit comedy Mattavilasa Prahasana, which pokes fun at Buddhist and Shaiva ascetics. The rivalry with the Chalukyas would shape Pallava history for the next century and a half.

events.text: 642: Narasimhavarman I takes Vatapi and Pulakeshin II is killed
events.detail: Narasimhavarman I came to the throne in 630. Pulakeshin II raided the Pallava north again but failed to take Kanchipuram, and Narasimhavarman beat the Chalukyas in several battles, including one at Manimangalam, about 20 miles east of Kanchi. He then carried the war into the Deccan. In 642 his army, led by the general Paranjothi, captured the Chalukya capital Vatapi (Badami), and Pulakeshin was killed. Narasimhavarman took the Tamil title Vatapikondan, 'he who conquered Vatapi', and the city never became a capital again.

events.text: c. 650: Narasimhavarman completes the monuments of Mamallapuram
events.detail: Narasimhavarman I completed the monuments that his father had begun at the port of Mamallapuram, which was named in his honour, among them the group of temples known as the Pancha Rathas. In 640 the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang had visited Kanchipuram, the Pallava capital. Narasimhavarman also twice sent an army to Sri Lanka to help the Sinhalese prince Manavarman, who had lived at his court, win the island's throne; the second expedition succeeded. Under him the Pallavas were at the peak of their power and fame.

events.text: c. 700: Rajasimha builds the Shore Temple and Kanchi's Kailasanatha temple
events.detail: After Mahendravarman II's brief reign, Paramesvaravarman I (c. 670–695) ruled, and in his time inscriptions in both Sanskrit and Tamil became common. His son Narasimhavarman II, known as Rajasimha (c. 695–728), is remembered as a builder in stone. He raised the Shore Temple at Mamallapuram, on the edge of the Bay of Bengal, and the Kailasanatha temple at Kanchipuram, one of the finest Pallava monuments, dates from his reign. His son Paramesvaravarman II ruled only briefly, and with his death in 731 the main line of the Pallavas came to an end.

events.text: 731: Nandivarman II of the Kadava branch is crowned at Kanchi as a boy
events.detail: When Paramesvaravarman II died without an heir, the throne passed to a collateral line. Nandivarman II, the son of Hiranyavarman of the Kadava family, was crowned at Kanchipuram while still a boy; one Chalukya account calls him a 13-year-old at the time of their invasion. His reign, which lasted until about 796, was one of the longest in Pallava history, but it was also full of danger, as the Chalukyas sought revenge for Vatapi and the Rashtrakutas rose in the Deccan. He took the title Pallavamalla.

events.text: c. 742: The Chalukya Vikramaditya II takes Kanchipuram but spares the city
events.detail: The Chalukyas had never forgotten the sack of their capital. Their king Vikramaditya II (c. 733–744) invaded the Pallava kingdom with help from the Western Gangas; the earliest record of the campaign, the Narwan plates, dates to 741 or 742. The young Nandivarman II fled Kanchipuram after a brief defence, leaving his regalia and war elephants behind. Vikramaditya 'entered Kanchi without destroying it', spared its people, returned spoils to the temples and made gifts recorded in a Kannada inscription in the Kailasanatha temple. The Chalukyas took Kanchi three times in all.

events.text: c. 846: Nandivarman III takes the throne and routs the Pandyas at Tellaru
events.detail: Nandivarman III, son of Dantivarman, ruled from about 846 to 869. The Pandya king Srimara Srivallabha had pushed into Pallava country, and Nandivarman formed a coalition with the Rashtrakutas and the Western Gangas against him. At Tellaru the allies defeated the Pandyas and chased them south to the Vaigai river; one account dates the battle to 830, before his accession, so its year is uncertain. Srimara later recovered most of his lands. Nandivarman kept a strong navy, and a Tamil inscription at Takua Pa in Thailand points to Pallava-era trade with South-east Asia.

events.text: 897: The Chola Aditya I kills Aparajita and annexes the Pallava kingdom
events.detail: After Nandivarman III his sons divided the kingdom, and its last king, Aparajita, ruled from about 880. The Pallavas' Chola feudatories had grown strong, and their king Aditya I (c. 871–907), once a Pallava ally, turned against his overlords. In 897 he invaded Tondai Nadu, the Pallava heartland around Kanchipuram, and killed Aparajita in battle. Tondaimandalam became part of the Chola realm, and Aditya went on to conquer the Kongu country. The Pallava dynasty, which had ruled from Kanchi for six centuries, came to an end.

name: Kadamba dynasty
summary: Mayurasharma founded the Kadamba kingdom c. 345 after breaking with the Pallavas of Kanchi, making Banavasi the capital of the first native kingdom of what is now Karnataka. It reached its height under Kakusthavarma, who tied his family by marriage to the Gangas, the Vakatakas and, by some accounts, the Guptas; around 455 it split into Banavasi and Triparvata branches, which were reunited c. 530. Soon after, c. 540, the rising Chalukyas of Badami overthrew their former overlords, and Kirtivarman I later annexed Banavasi itself.

events.text: Mayurasharma, who broke with the Pallavas c. 345, rules from Banavasi
events.detail: According to the Talagunda pillar inscription, Mayurasharma, a native of Talagunda, went to Kanchi, the Pallava capital, to study the Vedas. Humiliated there by a Pallava horseman, he gave up scholarship for the sword, built up a following in the forests of Shriparvata, defeated Pallava guards and made the Banas of Kolar pay tribute. The Pallava king reportedly recognised him as ruler of the land between the western ocean and the Malaprabha river. From his capital at Banavasi he ruled c. 345–365, founding the earliest native kingdom of present-day Karnataka, and performed horse sacrifices.

events.text: c. 365: Kangavarma succeeds and faces pressure from the Vakatakas
events.detail: Mayurasharma's son Kangavarma came to the throne around 365. The Vakatakas, the most powerful dynasty of the central Deccan, pressed on the young kingdom from the north. Historians disagree about the outcome: one view holds that he was defeated by the Vakataka king Prithvisena but kept his independence, another that his war with them had no lasting result. His son Bhagiratha, called lord of the Kadamba land in the Talagunda inscription, may have recovered earlier losses, although Vakataka records do not confirm this.

events.text: c. 435: Kakusthavarma's reign, the height of Kadamba power
events.detail: Bhagiratha's son Raghu died fighting the Pallavas, and his brother Kakusthavarma became king around 435. Historians regard his reign as the height of Kadamba power. He built a web of marriage alliances: one daughter married Madhava of the Western Ganga dynasty, another, Ajitabhattarika, married the Vakataka prince Narendrasena, and according to one historian a third married the Gupta emperor Skandagupta. These ties linked the Kadambas of Banavasi with leading houses of central and northern India. Tradition says the poet Kalidasa visited the Kadamba court, probably in Bhagiratha's time.

events.text: c. 450: The Halmidi inscription, the oldest known in Kannada, is carved
events.detail: A stone found in 1936 at the village of Halmidi in Hassan district is usually dated to about 450, though some scholars place it as late as the 6th century. Written in verse in pre-Old Kannada, it is described as the oldest known Kannada inscription. It records a grant of villages by two local governors to a prince, Vija-Arasa, for his military service, and names a King Kakustha, often identified with the Kadamba Kakusthavarma, though some epigraphists disagree. It is an early example of Kannada being used in government, alongside the Sanskrit of royal charters.

events.text: c. 455: Santivarma divides the kingdom; a Triparvata branch rules the south
events.detail: Kakusthavarma's son Santivarma, said to have worn three crowns as a sign of his prosperity, presided over the great Talagunda pillar inscription; his court poet Kubja composed and engraved it, telling the story of Mayurasharma. Santivarma's display drew Pallava attention, and around 455 he divided the kingdom: his younger brother Krishnavarma I took a southern branch, called Triparvata, while the senior line kept Banavasi in the north. Krishnavarma's sons later claimed that he had performed a horse sacrifice. The two branches ruled side by side, and in the end as rivals, for about 75 years.

events.text: c. 475: Mrigeshavarma wages successful wars on the Gangas and Pallavas
events.detail: In the Banavasi line, Shivamandhatru ruled for more than a decade from about 460, and Mrigeshavarma followed around 475. He fought the Pallavas and the Western Gangas with considerable success; his Halasi plates call him a destroyer of the Ganga family. He was also a patron of Jain institutions, continuing the Kadambas' support for several faiths. Meanwhile in the southern Triparvata branch, King Vishnuvarma is reported to have accepted Pallava overlordship, a sign of how the division had left the southern Kadambas exposed to their powerful eastern neighbour.

events.text: c. 519: Ravivarma's Davanagere record claims wide overlordship
events.detail: Ravivarma, who ruled roughly 485–519 (some lists say 497–537), restored Kadamba strength. He campaigned against the Pallavas, the Western Gangas and the Vakatakas, and a record from Davanagere dated around 519 is taken by the epigraphist D. C. Sircar as evidence of broad overlordship. He also granted land to a Buddhist community. Ravivarma left his brothers Bhanuvarma and Shivaratha to govern Halasi and Uchangi. His son Harivarma came to the throne around 519, according to the Sangolli inscription, and is described as a peaceful ruler.

events.text: c. 530: Krishnavarma II kills Harivarma and reunites the Kadamba kingdom
events.detail: The rivalry between the two Kadamba branches ended in bloodshed. According to the Bannahalli plates, Krishnavarma II of the southern Triparvata line raided Banavasi and killed King Harivarma around 530. With the senior line gone, the two halves of the kingdom were reunited under Krishnavarma, who had become the most prominent ruler of his branch. The reunion came late, however. In the north, the Chalukyas of Vatapi (Badami), a family that had served the Kadambas, were gathering strength and would soon turn on their overlords.

events.text: c. 540: The Chalukyas of Badami, once Kadamba vassals, conquer the kingdom
events.detail: Around 540 the Badami Chalukyas, who had been vassals of the Kadambas, conquered the kingdom, and the Kadambas in turn became vassals of the Chalukyas. Historians debate how the Chalukyas rose: K. A. Nilakanta Sastri thought their leader Pulakeshin I began as a Kadamba vassal and won independence by taking control of the Vatapi area, while others see him as a feudatory of a different house who took over former Kadamba territory. Later princes of the Triparvata line, such as Ajavarma and Bhogivarma, are still listed into the early 7th century.

events.text: 543: Pulakeshin I performs a horse sacrifice and fortifies Vatapi
events.detail: Pulakeshin I, the first sovereign Chalukya king (c. 543–566), proclaimed his independence in the grand manner. An inscription at Badami dated 543 records that he performed the Ashvamedha horse sacrifice, a claim to supreme kingship, and he made Vatapi his fortified capital. His son Kirtivarman I (c. 566–592) finished the work: he annexed the old Kadamba capital, Banavasi (Vaijayanti), and the Aihole inscription of Pulakeshin II later called him 'the night of doom' for the Kadambas. Kadamba rule as an independent kingdom was over, though later Kadamba families ruled Goa and Hangal for centuries.

name: Chalukyas of Badami
summary: Pulakeshin I made Vatapi (Badami) his fortress-capital in 543, and his grandson Pulakeshin II (c. 609–642) became master of most of the Deccan, defeating the northern emperor Harsha and founding a branch at Vengi in the east. The Pallavas sacked Badami in 642, but Vikramaditya I restored the kingdom in 655, and his successors raided Kanchipuram and adorned Pattadakal with temples. In 753 the Rashtrakuta vassal Dantidurga overthrew Kirtivarman II and ended the line.

events.text: Cave temples cut at Badami; a Kannada inscription is dated 578
events.detail: Pulakeshin I, a chief of the Chalukya family, made Vatapi (modern Badami) his capital in 543, choosing a site guarded by sandstone cliffs in northern Karnataka. Pulakeshin I fought the Kadambas of Banavasi, and his sons Kirtivarman I (566–597) and Mangalesha (597–609) went on enlarging the kingdom. In the cliffs above Badami the Chalukyas carved cave temples to Shiva and Vishnu; an inscription in one of them, in Kannada, is dated 578 and attributed to Mangalesha. These caves are among the earliest monuments of the Chalukya style of architecture.

events.text: c. 609: Pulakeshin II seizes the throne from his uncle Mangalesha
events.detail: Kirtivarman I had died while his son Pulakeshin was still young, so the throne passed to his brother Mangalesha. When Mangalesha tried to secure the succession for his own son, Pulakeshin fought and overthrew him, taking power around 609 (estimates range from 609 to 611). The new king first crushed rebels and then won back Banavasi from the Kadambas and forced the submission of the Alupas, the Gangas of Talakad and the Mauryas of the Konkan coast. Within a few years most of the western Deccan obeyed Badami.

events.text: Conquest of the eastern Deccan; Vengi given to Pulakeshin's brother
events.detail: Pulakeshin II then turned east. Around 616 he defeated the remnants of the Vishnukundina kingdom in coastal Andhra and also claimed Kalinga and Dakshina Kosala. In 621 he made his brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana viceroy of Vengi, the rich delta land between the Krishna and Godavari rivers. The kingdom now stretched from the Arabian Sea to the Bay of Bengal. After Pulakeshin's death the Vengi viceroyalty became independent, and Vishnuvardhana's descendants, the Eastern Chalukyas, ruled there for some four centuries.

events.text: c. 618–619: Pulakeshin II halts the emperor Harsha at the Narmada
events.detail: In the north, Harshavardhana of Kannauj had built an empire across the Ganges plain and sought to push south. Pulakeshin II met him on the Narmada river and defeated him, probably around 618–619, though some scholars date the war to the 630s. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang heard of the battle, and later Chalukya and Rashtrakuta records proudly recalled it. Pulakeshin's inscriptions also claim the submission of the Latas, Malavas and Gurjaras. The Narmada became the frontier between the two greatest Indian kingdoms of the age.

events.text: The Aihole inscription celebrates Pulakeshin II's conquests
events.detail: In 634 the court poet Ravikirti composed a Sanskrit praise poem for Pulakeshin II, carved in stone at Aihole, an early Chalukya temple town near Badami. The inscription lists the king's victories over the Kadambas, Gangas, Mauryas of the Konkan, Latas, Malavas and Gurjaras, his defeat of Harsha and his wars against the Pallavas. It is the main source for the reign and a landmark of classical Sanskrit poetry. At this moment the Chalukya kingdom was at its height, holding most of the Deccan.

events.text: c. 641–642: The pilgrim Xuanzang describes Pulakeshin's realm
events.detail: The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Xuanzang travelled through India in the 630s and 640s, and around 641–642 he passed through the Chalukya lands. He described a powerful and prosperous kingdom whose ruler was feared by his neighbours and commanded a large army, including war elephants. The Arab historian al-Tabari also reports diplomatic contact between Pulakeshin and the Persian king Khosrow II. Yet the long war with the Pallavas in the south was about to turn against the Chalukyas.

events.text: The Pallava king Narasimhavarman I captures Badami
events.detail: Pulakeshin II had invaded the Pallava kingdom of Kanchipuram several times with mixed results. Around 642 the Pallava king Narasimhavarman I struck back, marched deep into Chalukya territory and captured Vatapi itself. Pulakeshin is presumed to have been killed in the fighting. The Pallavas occupied Badami for about thirteen years, a humiliation the Pallavas long celebrated. The Chalukya kingdom fell into confusion, with several of Pulakeshin's sons ruling parts of it in turn, and the eastern viceroyalty at Vengi went its own way.

events.text: Vikramaditya I drives out the Pallavas and restores the kingdom
events.detail: Pulakeshin's son Vikramaditya I rebuilt Chalukya power. By 655 he had expelled the Pallavas from Badami, brought rebellious vassals back under control and reunited the kingdom; he took the title Rajamalla. He ruled until 680 and carried the war back into Pallava country. His son Vinayaditya (680–696) and grandson Vijayaditya (696–733) kept the restored kingdom strong. Vijayaditya's long reign was a peaceful and prosperous time, remembered above all for temple building.

events.text: c. 725: Temples rise at Pattadakal, the Chalukya royal centre
events.detail: Vijayaditya's long reign (696–733) was a prosperous time, remembered for its temple building. The Chalukyas built a group of grand stone temples at Pattadakal, on the Malaprabha river near Badami, and the Sangameshvara temple there dates to about 725. Later kings and queens added more, including the Galaganatha temple of about 740 and the Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna temples of about 740–745. Pattadakal, with Aihole and Badami, became the showcase of Chalukya wealth and devotion in stone.

events.text: Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin defeats an Arab army in Gujarat
events.detail: In the early 8th century the armies of the Umayyad Caliphate, based in Sind, raided deep into western India. Around 739 an Arab force from Sind advanced into southern Gujarat, the Lata country governed by a branch of the Chalukya family based at Navsari. The governor, Avanijanashraya Pulakeshin, defeated it and drove it out. The victory helped stop the Arab advance into the Deccan, and the Chalukya king Vikramaditya II honoured him with the title Avanijanashraya, 'refuge of the people of the earth'.

events.text: c. 740: Vikramaditya II enters Kanchipuram, the Pallava capital
events.detail: Vikramaditya II (c. 733–746) carried the old feud with the Pallavas to its climax. After 734 he invaded their kingdom, defeated Nandivarman II and entered Kanchipuram; the Narwan plates of 741 or 742 are the earliest record of the campaign. He is said to have taken the city three times in all. Rather than plunder it, he returned treasure to its temples, recorded in a Kannada inscription in the Kailasanatha temple. To mark his victory his queens built the Virupaksha and Mallikarjuna temples at Pattadakal.

events.text: The Rashtrakuta vassal Dantidurga overthrows Kirtivarman II
events.detail: Kirtivarman II succeeded his father in 746, but the Chalukya kingdom had been weakened by decades of war with the Pallavas, and its northern vassals were growing strong. One of them, the Rashtrakuta chief Dantidurga, ruled lands in the northern Deccan around Ellora. In 753 he defeated Kirtivarman II, according to his Samangadh copper-plate grant, and took over the northern Chalukya lands. Kirtivarman held on in the south for a short time, but the Badami Chalukya line was finished, and the Rashtrakutas became the new masters of the Deccan.

reigns.name: Pallava occupation of Badami; rival sons of Pulakeshin II

name: Harsha's Empire (Pushyabhuti dynasty)
summary: Harsha of the Pushyabhuti family, crowned king of Thanesar in 606, ruled the plains of northern India from Kannauj, with kings from Valabhi to Kamarupa accepting his overlordship. His drive south was stopped at the Narmada by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II in 618–19, and the Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang left a vivid picture of his court. Harsha died without an heir in 647; a usurper seized Kannauj, and the empire fell apart.

events.text: c. 612: Harsha, crowned in 606, rules the northern plains from Kannauj
events.detail: Harsha's father Prabhakaravardhana ruled the small kingdom of Thanesar, north of Delhi, and died around 605. His elder son Rajyavardhana was soon killed by the king of Gauda (Bengal), usually identified as Shashanka, and in April 606 the sixteen-year-old Harsha was crowned. Older historians dated his conquests to 606–612, following the pilgrim Xuanzang's remark that he subdued the 'Five Indias', but the wars probably went on for years. Harsha made Kannauj (Kanyakubja) his capital. Rulers from Valabhi in the west to Kamarupa in the east came to accept his overlordship.

events.text: Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas defeats Harsha on the Narmada
events.detail: With the north under his control, Harsha looked south to the Deccan, ruled by the Chalukya king Pulakeshin II. In the winter of 618–19 the two armies met on the banks of the Narmada river. Pulakeshin's Aihole inscription boasts that Harsha's joy 'melted away by fear' as his war elephants fell; a Chalukya grant dated April 619 already celebrates the victory. Harsha retreated, and the Narmada became the frontier between the two empires. Harsha's realm would stay a northern empire, never reaching into the Deccan.

events.text: c. 630: Chinese monk Xuanzang arrives in India; he studies at Nalanda
events.detail: Xuanzang, a Buddhist monk from Tang China, set out around 629 to find Buddhist texts at their source. He spent about thirteen years in India, roughly 630 to 644, travelling widely and studying at the great monastery of Nalanda under the teacher Shilabhadra. His later travel book, the Great Tang Records on the Western Regions, is one of the main sources for Harsha's reign. Xuanzang describes Harsha as ruling from Kanyakubja (Kannauj) and praises his justice and generosity, though he wrote as an admiring guest.

events.text: c. 636: Shashanka of Gauda dies; Harsha and Kamarupa divide his kingdom
events.detail: Shashanka, king of Gauda in Bengal with his capital at Karnasuvarna, was Harsha's great enemy in the east, blamed for the death of Harsha's brother. To fight him, Harsha allied with Bhaskaravarman, king of Kamarupa (Assam). Harsha's attacks never broke Shashanka, who kept his kingdom until his death, dated about 636 (some sources say 625). His son Manava ruled for only eight months. Gauda was then divided between Harsha and Bhaskaravarman, carrying Harsha's power into Bengal.

events.text: A Tang mission with Wang Xuance meets Harsha in Magadha
events.detail: Harsha opened diplomatic contact with the Tang dynasty of China by sending an envoy to its court. In reply, Emperor Taizong sent a mission in 643 led by Li Yibiao, with Wang Xuance as his assistant. The Chinese envoys met Harsha in Magadha, in what is now Bihar. The exchange linked Harsha's court with the Tang capital at Chang'an, a world away across the Himalayas. These contacts would bring Wang Xuance back to India a few years later, at a very different moment.

events.text: c. 643: Harsha hosts a great religious assembly at Kannauj
events.detail: Harsha was a patron of Buddhism as well as of other faiths. Late in Xuanzang's stay, around 643, Harsha asked the pilgrim to come to Kannauj for a great Buddhist assembly. Kings of neighbouring states attended, together with Buddhist monks, Hindus and Jains. Harsha was by then an ally of Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa, whose court Xuanzang had just visited. The assembly showed off Harsha's power as overlord: subordinate kings came to his capital and joined his ceremonies, a sign of how far his authority reached.

events.text: c. 643: Harsha gives away his treasure at the Prayag gathering
events.detail: After the Kannauj assembly, Harsha invited Xuanzang to the great gathering at Prayag (Allahabad), where the Ganges and Yamuna meet, a festival linked with the Kumbha Mela. Xuanzang watched the emperor hand out gifts on a huge scale to the poor and to religious men, an act of royal generosity Harsha was said to repeat every few years. Xuanzang then returned with him to Kannauj, received a grand farewell, and left for China, reaching Chang'an early in 645.

events.text: Harsha dies without an heir; Arunasva seizes the throne of Kannauj
events.detail: Harsha died in 647, possibly at Kannauj, aged about 57. He left no son, and the Pushyabhuti dynasty ended with him. A man named Arunasva usurped the throne of Kannauj. When a new Tang embassy under Wang Xuance arrived, Arunasva's forces attacked it, and Wang escaped overnight to Nepal. Without Harsha himself, the network of loyal and subordinate kings that held his empire together quickly dissolved, and northern India broke back into rival kingdoms.

events.text: Wang Xuance's Tibetan and Nepalese army captures Arunasva
events.detail: From Nepal, Wang Xuance raised an army with the help of the Tibetan emperor Songtsen Gampo and the Nepalese king Narendradeva: about 1,200 Tibetan soldiers and more than 7,000 Nepalese cavalry. In 648 they attacked Arunasva at a place the Chinese called Chabuheluo. According to the Old Book of Tang the fighting lasted three days; Arunasva fled, was captured, and was taken back to China as a prisoner. The episode marked the end of Harsha's empire: no single power ruled the northern plains again for decades.

name: Gurjara-Pratihara Empire
summary: The Gurjara-Pratiharas rose in Rajasthan and Malwa around 730, winning fame for holding back the Arab armies of Sind. After decades of war with the Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan over Kannauj, Nagabhata II took the city, and under Mihira Bhoja and Mahendrapala I (836–910) the empire ruled most of the northern plains. Rashtrakuta raids, breakaway vassals and Mahmud of Ghazni's sack of Kannauj in 1018 reduced it to a small kingdom that ended around 1036.

events.text: c. 738: Nagabhata I joins the kings who turn back the Arab armies of Sind
events.detail: In the 720s and 730s the Umayyad governors of Sind sent armies into Rajasthan and Gujarat. The Pratihara dynasty, which probably began in the Jalore–Bhinmal area and spread to Ujjain, emerged as a leader of the resistance under its founder Nagabhata I. Many historians believe he repulsed the Arabs near Ujjain, though where he fought them is uncertain; in 738–39 a Chalukya army decisively beat them at Navsari in Gujarat. By 743 the Arabs had lost their conquests in Rajasthan and Gujarat, and the Pratiharas had a firm base in western India.

events.text: c. 786: Vatsaraja takes Kannauj and beats Dharmapala, then falls to Dhruva
events.detail: Kannauj, the old capital of Harsha, was the prize of northern India, and three powers fought for it: the Pratiharas, the Palas of Bengal and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan. Around 785–790 the Pratihara king Vatsaraja forced the ruler of Kannauj to accept his overlordship and sent an army that defeated the Pala king Dharmapala. But the Rashtrakuta king Dhruva crossed the Narmada and defeated Vatsaraja, then Dharmapala too, before going home in 790. This 'tripartite struggle' would last for a generation.

events.text: c. 799: Rashtrakuta Govinda III defeats Nagabhata II near Gwalior
events.detail: Vatsaraja's son Nagabhata II faced another Rashtrakuta invasion. Around 798–800 the Rashtrakuta king Govinda III marched north, defeated Nagabhata near Gwalior and conquered Malwa and other lands. The ruler of Kannauj, Chakrayudha, surrendered, and Dharmapala of Bengal also submitted. Like his father, Govinda soon returned to the Deccan, but the Pratiharas lost Malwa and Gujarat for a time. Nagabhata later recovered Malwa, and the Rashtrakuta threat ended when Govinda died in 814.

events.text: c. 810–816: Nagabhata II takes Kannauj and routs Dharmapala at Munger
events.detail: Freed from Rashtrakuta pressure, Nagabhata II invaded the Ganges–Yamuna Doab, defeated Chakrayudha, the Pala-backed king of Kannauj, and took the city. He then fought Dharmapala himself near Munger, in Bihar, and won a decisive victory. One account dates this to 816, but a Rashtrakuta inscription from Baroda dated 812 already records his victory over the Pala king. The Pratiharas had won the long struggle: Kannauj became their capital for two centuries.

events.text: Mihira Bhoja becomes emperor; the Pratiharas reach their height
events.detail: Mihira Bhoja, who followed the short reign of Ramabhadra, ruled from Kannauj from about 836 to 885 and took the title Adivaraha, which appears on his coins. Between 833 and 842 Pratihara forces drove the Arabs out of Kutch. After the death of the Pala king Devapala, Bhoja defeated his successor Narayanapala and pushed east. At its height his empire reached the Narmada in the south, the Sutlej in the northwest and the edge of Bengal in the east, making it the greatest power in northern India.

events.text: Arab traveller Sulaiman praises the Gurjara king's cavalry
events.detail: Arab merchants and geographers who traded with India wrote about its kingdoms. The account attributed to Sulaiman, written around 851, described the 'Gurjara' king, meaning the Pratihara emperor: 'The ruler of Gurjara maintains numerous forces and no other Indian prince has so fine a cavalry.' The same account described the Pala kingdom of Bengal, which it called Ruhmi. The description fits Mihira Bhoja's reign, when Pratihara armies guarded the western frontier against the Arab states of Sind and fought rivals to the east and south.

events.text: c. 880: Rashtrakuta Krishna II defeats Bhoja's army at Ujjain
events.detail: The Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas still competed for Gujarat and Malwa. Mihira Bhoja intervened in a succession struggle among the Rashtrakutas' Gujarat branch; his cavalry raid was repulsed, but he kept parts of Gujarat and Malwa. Around 880, or at least before 888, the Rashtrakuta king Krishna II defeated the Pratiharas at Ujjain, the main city of Malwa. The setback did not last: by the end of his reign Bhoja had ended the Gujarat Rashtrakuta line, and the empire's southwestern frontier held.

events.text: Mahendrapala I succeeds; his empire runs from the Himalayas to the Vindhyas
events.detail: Mihira Bhoja is thought to have died around 885, and his son Mahendrapala I ruled until about 910. He kept his father's empire intact and pushed its frontiers further east; the historian R. C. Majumdar describes it as stretching from the Himalayas to the Vindhya range. An unclear verse in the Kashmiri chronicle Rajatarangini hints that he may have lost some land in the Punjab to Kashmir. His teacher, the poet Rajashekhara, called him the great king of Aryavarta and celebrated the splendour of Kannauj.

events.text: c. 916: Rashtrakuta Indra III sacks Kannauj; Mahipala I flees
events.detail: After Mahendrapala's death the Pratihara royal family quarrelled over the throne. The Rashtrakuta king Indra III, crowned in 915, took advantage. He marched north into the Ganges–Yamuna Doab and attacked Kannauj, while his vassal chased the Pratihara emperor Mahipala I, who, a Kannada poet wrote, 'fled as if struck by lightning'. Kannauj was badly damaged and held by the Rashtrakutas until about 916. The Pratiharas soon regained their capital, but the blow to their prestige was lasting.

events.text: c. 950: The Chandelas take Gwalior as vassal kingdoms break away
events.detail: Mahipala I still claimed a wide empire, but after him a series of short reigns weakened the dynasty. Its vassal families, once loyal governors and allies, began to act as independent kings: the Paramaras in Malwa, the Chandelas in Bundelkhand, the Kalachuris, the Tomaras around Delhi and the Chahamanas in Rajasthan. Around 950 the Chandelas seized the great fortress of Gwalior. By the late 10th century the Pratiharas held little more than the region around Kannauj.

events.text: Mahmud of Ghazni captures Kannauj; King Rajyapala flees
events.detail: Mahmud of Ghazni, ruler of a Turkic empire based in Afghanistan, led repeated raids into northern India in search of plunder. In 1018 he marched on Kannauj. The Pratihara king Rajyapala abandoned the city and fled, and Mahmud captured it. The Chandela king Vidyadhara later had Rajyapala killed and placed Trilochanapala on the Pratihara throne as his puppet. The once-imperial dynasty, which had ruled the northern plains a century earlier, now depended on the favour of its own former vassals.

events.text: Yasahpala, the last known Pratihara king, dies
events.detail: After Trilochanapala, the last known ruler of the dynasty was Yasahpala, who reigned from about 1024 until his death in 1036. By then the Pratiharas held only a small territory around Kannauj and lived in the shadow of the Chandelas and other former vassals. With Yasahpala the line that had defended the west against the Arabs and ruled Kannauj for two centuries disappears from the records. Its lands passed to the regional kingdoms that had grown out of its former provinces.

name: Pala Empire
summary: The Palas began around 750, when the chiefs of Bengal chose Gopala as king to end years of anarchy. Dharmapala and Devapala made Bengal and Bihar the base of a great Buddhist empire that fought the Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas for Kannauj and built the monasteries of Vikramashila and Somapura. After losing the west and much of Bengal in the 10th century, the Palas revived under Mahipala I and Ramapala, but the Sena dynasty pushed them out of Bengal in the 1150s and their line faded by about 1162.

events.text: c. 750: Bengal's chiefs choose Gopala as king, ending years of anarchy
events.detail: In the early 8th century Bengal had no strong ruler. Local chiefs fought one another, a state of chaos later remembered as matsya nyaya, the 'law of the fish', where the big fish eat the small. Around 750 the chiefs agreed to choose one of their number, Gopala, as king. He ended the disorder and founded the Pala dynasty, which would rule Bengal and Bihar for some four centuries. Gopala ruled until about 770–775, laying the foundation for his son's expansion.

events.text: c. 786: Pratihara and Rashtrakuta armies defeat Dharmapala
events.detail: Gopala's son Dharmapala wanted to control Kannauj, the leading city of the northern plains. So did the Pratiharas of western India and the Rashtrakutas of the Deccan. Around 785–790 the Pratihara king Vatsaraja sent an army into Bengal that defeated Dharmapala. Then the Rashtrakuta king Dhruva defeated Vatsaraja and beat Dharmapala in the Ganges–Yamuna Doab. Dhruva went back south in 790, however, and in the end the Pala king gained more than he had lost.

events.text: c. 791: Dharmapala installs Chakrayudha at Kannauj before an assembly of kings
events.detail: With his rivals gone, Dharmapala marched on Kannauj around 791, removed its king Indrayudha and installed his own nominee, Chakrayudha. His Khalimpur copper plate says the rulers of Bhoja, Matsya, Madra, Kuru, Yadu, Yavana, Avanti, Gandhara and Kira attended the ceremony and accepted it. These kings probably kept their own lands and only recognised Dharmapala as overlord, and the claim may be exaggerated. Still, for a time the Pala king was the most powerful ruler in northern India.

events.text: c. 800: Dharmapala founds Vikramashila and builds the Somapura monastery
events.detail: The Palas were great patrons of Buddhism. Dharmapala founded the monastery of Vikramashila, on the Ganges near Bhagalpur in Bihar, in the late 8th or early 9th century; it became one of the main centres of Buddhist learning in Asia. He also built the Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur, in today's Bangladesh, the largest of the Pala-era monasteries and a World Heritage Site since 1985. Scholars from these monasteries, such as Atisha, later carried Pala Buddhism to Tibet.

events.text: c. 810–816: Nagabhata II defeats Dharmapala at Munger; Kannauj is lost
events.detail: Around 798–800 the Rashtrakuta king Govinda III invaded the north, and Dharmapala and his protégé at Kannauj submitted to him. After Govinda went home, the Pratihara king Nagabhata II attacked. He took Kannauj from Chakrayudha and then defeated Dharmapala's army near Munger, in Bihar. One account dates the battle to 816; a Rashtrakuta inscription of 812 already mentions the Pala defeat. Kannauj passed to the Pratiharas for good, and the Palas' western ambitions shrank back toward Bihar.

events.text: c. 812: Devapala succeeds his father; Pala power reaches its height
events.detail: Dharmapala's son Devapala ruled for about forty years, from around 810–821 to 850–861 depending on the historian. His inscriptions claim wide conquests: the king of Pragjyotisha (Assam) submitted without a fight, the Utkalas of Odisha were crushed, and he defeated the 'Gurjaras', meaning the Pratihara king Bhoja I. Some of these claims are probably exaggerated, but his reign marked the greatest extent of Pala power. He also granted villages for a Nalanda monastery requested by the Sailendra king of Java.

events.text: c. 860: Mihira Bhoja of the Pratiharas pushes the Palas back east
events.detail: Devapala's death around 850 left the Palas exposed. The Pratihara emperor Mihira Bhoja, ruling from Kannauj, defeated the new Pala king Narayanapala and pushed east into lands near Gorakhpur. Narayanapala ruled for a long time, until about 908, but the Palas were now on the defensive. The great conquests of Dharmapala and Devapala in the west were lost, and the Pratiharas became the leading power of the northern plains, with the Palas confined to Bihar and Bengal.

events.text: c. 970: Kamboja rulers seize northwestern Bengal as the Pala realm breaks up
events.detail: In the 10th century the Pala kingdom came under attack from Kamarupa (Assam) and the Chandelas of Bundelkhand. Amid these invasions a family calling itself Kamboja took power in northwestern and southwestern Bengal, around Gauda, Burdwan and Midnapore, probably under Gopala II or Vigrahapala II (c. 960–986). Its origins are disputed, and some historians think its founder was himself a Pala prince. Raids by the Chandela king Dhanga and the Chandra king Kalyanachandra added to the turmoil, and the Pala realm broke apart.

events.text: c. 988: Mahipala I recovers north and east Bengal for the Palas
events.detail: Mahipala I, who came to the throne around 988 (some scholars say 978), led a Pala revival. His Bangar charter says he won back nearly all of north and east Bengal 'after defeating the usurpers who had seized his ancestral kingdom', thought to mean the Kambojas, who had been weakened by Chandela and Chandra attacks. He held Bihar as well and, by some accounts, pushed the Pala frontier as far as Varanasi. For a few decades the Palas were again a major power.

events.text: c. 1022: Rajendra Chola's northern army defeats Mahipala I
events.detail: The Chola emperor Rajendra I of south India sent a great army north along the east coast, through Odisha into Bengal, between about 1021 and 1023. It defeated several local rulers, including the last Kamboja king of Dandabhukti, and then Mahipala himself, carrying off booty such as elephants and treasure. The Cholas raided rather than conquered and soon went home, but the invasion hampered Mahipala's revival and showed how exposed Bengal was.

events.text: c. 1075: Kaivarta rebels under Divya kill Mahipala II and take Varendra
events.detail: Mahipala II, who had imprisoned his younger brothers Shurapala and Ramapala, faced a revolt by the Kaivartas, a community of north Bengal led by their chief Divya. Around 1075 Divya killed Mahipala II and took Varendra, the Palas' heartland in north Bengal, which Kaivarta chiefs, later including Bhima, went on to rule as their own kingdom. The two brothers escaped and reigned in turn, Shurapala for two years and then Ramapala. The Palas now risked losing still more land to the rebels.

events.text: Ramapala becomes king; he will win Varendra back from the Kaivartas
events.detail: Ramapala became king around 1077. Lacking a strong army, he won over powerful local chiefs with offers of gold and land. His cousin Sivaraja crossed the Padma river and devastated Varendra; Ramapala followed, and in a pitched battle the Kaivarta leader Bhima was captured and later executed. Ramapala ruled from a new capital, Ramavati, and brought Kamarupa and Rarh under his control, though he lost Mithila. His court poet Sandhyakar Nandi celebrated him in the Ramacharitam. It was the last great age of the Palas.

events.text: c. 1153: Vijaya Sena drives Madanapala out of Gauda
events.detail: After Ramapala's death in 1130 his successors Kumarapala, Gopala and Madanapala ruled a shrinking kingdom. One of Ramapala's allies, the Sena chief Vijaya Sena of Rarh in western Bengal, had won his independence and grew stronger. Pala records continue to Madanapala's eighth year, 1152–53, after which Vijaya Sena most probably defeated him and took the throne of Gauda. The Palas lost Bengal, the land where their dynasty began, and kept only parts of Bihar.

events.text: Madanapala's reign ends; Pala rule fades out in Bihar
events.detail: Madanapala, the last widely recognised Pala king, ruled until about 1162. After him, kings named Govindapala and Palapala ruled parts of the Gaya district of Bihar until about 1200, though their link to the imperial Palas is uncertain. The Sena king Ballala Sena is credited with finally defeating Govindapala. After four centuries the Pala dynasty, which had ruled Bengal and Bihar and spread Buddhist learning across Asia, came to an end.

name: Rashtrakuta dynasty
summary: Dantidurga overthrew the Chalukyas of Badami in 753, and his successors built an empire from the Kaveri to the Narmada, carving the Kailasa temple at Ellora and marching north to Kannauj three times in the struggle with the Palas and Pratiharas. Amoghavarsha I ruled from Manyakheta for 64 years, and Krishna III humbled the Cholas at Takkolam in 949. After Malwa's army sacked Manyakheta in 972, the vassal Tailapa II seized power in 973, and the last claimant, Indra IV, died in 982.

events.text: Dantidurga, victor over the Badami Chalukyas in 753, rules the Deccan
events.detail: The Rashtrakutas were a family of Chalukya vassals in the northern Deccan. Their chief Dantidurga took advantage of the Chalukyas' long, draining wars with the Pallavas. In 753, according to his Samangadh copper-plate grant, he defeated the Chalukya king Kirtivarman II and took the northern Chalukya lands, the founding moment of the Rashtrakuta empire. Dantidurga died about 756 without a son, and his uncle Krishna I succeeded him, finishing the destruction of Chalukya power in the south.

events.text: c. 760s: Krishna I has the Kailasa temple carved from the rock at Ellora
events.detail: Krishna I (c. 756–774) extended Rashtrakuta rule over most of present-day Karnataka and the Konkan coast. He is generally credited with the Kailasa temple at Ellora, a whole Shiva temple cut downward out of a single basalt cliff, though the inscriptions linking it to him are not certain proof. Its tower rises about 33 metres above the courtyard. It is the largest of Ellora's 34 cave temples and is seen as the peak of Indian rock-cut architecture, a statement of the new dynasty's wealth and confidence.

events.text: Dhruva Dharavarsha takes power and leads the first raid on Kannauj
events.detail: Krishna I's son Govinda II was pushed aside in 780 by his brother Dhruva Dharavarsha, a vigorous soldier. Dhruva expanded the kingdom to cover the land between the Kaveri river and central India. He then joined the contest for Kannauj, the old imperial city of the Ganges plain, which the Pratiharas of the west and the Palas of Bengal were fighting over. He defeated both rivals and returned with rich booty, but took no lasting territory. This three-way war is known as the Tripartite Struggle.
