events.text: c. 800: Govinda III marches north; Pratiharas and Palas submit
events.detail: Dhruva's son Govinda III (793–814) first crushed a revolt by his elder brother Stambha and twelve allied kings. Around 800 he invaded the north and won the submission of the Pratihara emperor Nagabhata II, the Pala emperor Dharmapala and Chakrayudha, ruler of Kannauj; a later inscription boasts that his horses drank from Himalayan streams. He also put his brother Indra in charge of Gujarat, and the Cholas, Pandyas and Keralas paid him tribute. Under Govinda III the empire reached the height of its military power.

events.text: Amoghavarsha I becomes king at about 14 and survives early revolts
events.detail: When Govinda III died in 814, his son Amoghavarsha I was only about fourteen. Relatives and vassals rebelled and briefly drove him from power, but with the help of his cousin Karka he regained control by 821. He then made peace with the Western Gangas through marriage alliances and fought the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, defeating them at Vingavalli. Amoghavarsha went on to reign for about 64 years, one of the longest precisely dated reigns of any monarch.

events.text: c. 850: Kavirajamarga, Kannada's oldest surviving literary work, at Manyakheta
events.detail: Amoghavarsha I moved the capital to Manyakheta (modern Malkhed in Karnataka), which remained the Rashtrakuta capital until the empire's end. His court was a centre of learning. The Kavirajamarga, a work on poetics written around 850 and credited to the king or his court poet, is the earliest surviving work of Kannada literature. The mathematician Mahaviracharya dedicated his book to Amoghavarsha. A devout Jain who also supported Hindu temples, the king is sometimes called the 'Ashoka of the South' for his peaceable rule.

events.text: An Arab account ranks the Rashtrakutas among the world's four great empires
events.detail: Arab merchants traded along India's west coast, which the Rashtrakutas controlled. An Arabic travel account dated 851, the Silsilat al-Tawarikh, associated with the merchant Sulaiman, counted the Rashtrakuta kingdom among the four principal empires of the world, and the merchant Sulaiman named its king, Amoghavarsha I, among the world's four great kings. The judgement reflected the empire's size, its large armies and its wealth from trade, and the welcome it gave foreign merchants.

events.text: Krishna II's reign begins; the empire shrinks after a Vengi revolt
events.detail: Amoghavarsha I died in 878 and was succeeded by his son Krishna II, who ruled until 914. His reign was a time of setbacks. The Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi, in coastal Andhra, rose in revolt and fought the Rashtrakutas for years, and the empire shrank. There were wars also with the Pratiharas in the north and the Cholas in the south. The Rashtrakutas remained a great power, but the far-flung empire of Govinda III could not be held together without constant fighting.

events.text: c. 916: Indra III sacks Kannauj, the Pratihara capital
events.detail: Krishna II's grandson Indra III, crowned in 915, saw a chance in the family quarrels of the Pratihara rulers of Kannauj. He first drove a Pratihara vassal from Govardhana near Nasik, making the Paramaras of Malwa his own vassals, then struck deep into the Ganges–Yamuna doab. The Pratihara emperor Mahipala I fled, pursued by Indra's Chalukya vassal Narasimha, who 'bathed his horses in the Ganges'. Kannauj was destroyed and held until about 916. The raid weakened the Pratiharas for good but added no lasting territory.

events.text: Krishna III defeats the Cholas at Takkolam and overruns their north
events.detail: Krishna III (939–967) was the last great Rashtrakuta king. In the south the Cholas of Thanjavur had grown powerful. In 948–949 Krishna, with his Western Ganga ally Butuga II, met a Chola army under the crown prince Rajaditya at Takkolam, near Kanchipuram. Rajaditya was killed, reportedly by an arrow from Butuga, and the Cholas were routed. The Rashtrakutas took the northern Chola province of Tondaimandalam, Krishna styled himself 'conqueror of Tanjore', and his armies reached Rameswaram. The empire now stretched from the Narmada to the Kaveri.

events.text: Siyaka of Malwa sacks the Rashtrakuta capital, Manyakheta
events.detail: After Krishna III died in 967, his brother Khottiga came to the throne, and the vassals began to drift away. The Paramaras of Malwa, once Rashtrakuta vassals, had grown strong north of the Narmada. In 972 the Paramara king Siyaka Harsha invaded, defeated the Rashtrakuta army and plundered Manyakheta itself. The sack shattered the dynasty's prestige. Khottiga died soon afterwards, and his nephew Karka II inherited an empire whose vassals no longer feared it.

events.text: The vassal Tailapa II overthrows Karka II and seizes the empire
events.detail: Tailapa II governed Tardavadi, in the Bijapur region, as a Rashtrakuta vassal and claimed descent from the old Chalukyas of Badami. In 973 he overthrew the weakened emperor Karka II and took the throne, founding the Western Chalukya dynasty and making Manyakheta his capital. Many former Rashtrakuta vassals, such as the Shilaharas of the Konkan, accepted him as overlord. The Rashtrakuta empire passed almost whole into the hands of the new dynasty, roughly two centuries after the Rashtrakutas had displaced the Chalukyas.

events.text: Indra IV, the last Rashtrakuta, fasts to death at Shravanabelagola
events.detail: Indra IV, a member of the Rashtrakuta royal house, carried on as a claimant to the throne after 973, but he could not defeat Tailapa II. Giving up the struggle, he turned to the Jain faith of many of his ancestors. On 20 March 982 he died by sallekhana, the Jain ritual fast to death, at the hill shrine of Shravanabelagola in southern Karnataka. With him the Rashtrakuta dynasty came to an end, and the Western Chalukyas ruled the whole of its former Deccan empire.

name: Chandela dynasty of Jejakabhukti
summary: The Chandelas of Jejakabhukti (Bundelkhand) rose from vassals of the Gurjara-Pratiharas to sovereign kings under Dhanga in the later 10th century, ruling from Khajuraho, the fortress of Kalanjara and later Mahoba. Vidyadhara stood up to Mahmud of Ghazni in 1019 and 1022, but Kalachuri attacks, the sack of Mahoba by Prithviraj Chauhan in c. 1182–83 and the Delhi Sultanate's capture of Kalanjara in 1202–03 wore the kingdom down. Trailokyavarman won back much of the old domain, yet by the time of Hammiravarman (c. 1288–1311) the kings had dropped their imperial titles, and the main line ended around 1315.

events.text: Under Dhanga (r. c. 950–999), the Chandelas throw off Pratihara overlordship
events.detail: The Chandelas began in the 9th century as a small kingdom around Khajuraho, ruling as vassals of the Gurjara-Pratiharas of Kannauj. As Pratihara power weakened, Yashovarman (c. 925–950) became practically independent, captured the great fort of Kalanjara and commissioned the Lakshmana Temple at Khajuraho. His son Dhanga, who reigned from about 950 to 999, went further. His inscriptions no longer name a Pratihara overlord, which historians read as a formal claim to sovereignty. The Chandelas now ruled the Vindhyan country of Bundelkhand in their own right and became one of the leading powers of northern India.

events.text: c. 999: Dhanga dies, leaving the Vishvanatha temple at Khajuraho
events.detail: Dhanga's reign of almost half a century was remembered as a high point of Chandela power. Court inscriptions boast of conquests far to the east and south, and claim that the rulers of Kosala and other lands obeyed the commands of his officers, though historians treat such claims as poetic exaggeration. At Khajuraho he built the Vishvanatha Temple, dedicated to Shiva, one of the finest of the town's sandstone temples. Dhanga died around 999. His son Ganda held the kingdom together for a few years before Vidyadhara, the most powerful of the Chandela kings, succeeded him.

events.text: c. 1018: Vidyadhara punishes the king of Kannauj for fleeing Mahmud of Ghazni
events.detail: In about 1018 Mahmud of Ghazni marched deep into northern India and sacked Kannauj, the old Pratihara capital, after its king, possibly Rajyapala, fled. The Arab historian Ibn al-Athir says that 'Bida', king of Khajuraho, a form of Vidyadhara's name, then killed the Kannauj king as punishment for his cowardice. An inscription at Dubkund credits the deed to Arjuna of the Kachchhapaghata family, who probably acted for Vidyadhara as his ally or vassal. The episode showed that the Chandelas, not the fading Pratiharas, now led the defence of the Ganges plain, and it set Vidyadhara on a collision course with Mahmud.

events.text: Mahmud of Ghazni marches against Vidyadhara; the Chandela army withdraws
events.detail: Mahmud returned in 1019 to punish Vidyadhara. On the way he defeated the Kabul Shahi ruler Trilochanapala and sacked Bari, the new Pratihara capital, before meeting the Chandela army. The chroniclers disagree about what followed. Nizamuddin Ahmad says there was no battle: Vidyadhara slipped away at night, leaving his camp to be plundered, including 580 elephants. Ibn al-Athir instead describes a battle that ended at nightfall. Either way the Chandela kingdom survived intact, and Mahmud went home with booty rather than new territory.

events.text: Mahmud besieges Gwalior and Kalanjara; Vidyadhara makes peace with elephants
events.detail: In 1022 Mahmud invaded again. He first besieged Gwalior, held by Vidyadhara's Kachchhapaghata vassal Kirtiraja, and lifted the siege after four days for 35 elephants. He then laid a long siege to Kalanjara, the Chandela stronghold. According to the Muslim chronicles, Vidyadhara offered 300 elephants and asked for safety, and Firishta adds that Mahmud gave him fifteen fortresses in return. The historian S. K. Mitra reads the deal as an exchange of gifts. Vidyadhara, who also commissioned the Kandariya Mahadeva Temple at Khajuraho, kept a kingdom stretching from the Chambal to the Narmada.

events.text: c. 1050: Kalachuri Lakshmi-Karna subjugates the Chandela king Devavarman
events.detail: By the end of Vidyadhara's reign the Ghaznavid wars had weakened the kingdom. Its southern neighbours, the Kalachuris of Tripuri near modern Jabalpur, took advantage. Their king Gangeya-deva conquered the eastern parts of the Chandela lands, although Vidyadhara's successor Vijayapala is said to have beaten him in battle. Gangeya's son Lakshmi-Karna went further and subjugated Vijayapala's son Devavarman, who reigned c. 1050–1060. For a time the Chandelas lived in the shadow of the Kalachuris, and their power shrank back towards the core of Bundelkhand.

events.text: c. 1070: Kirttivarman defeats Lakshmi-Karna and revives the kingdom
events.detail: Devavarman's brother Kirttivarman, who reigned c. 1060–1100, restored Chandela fortunes. A Mahoba inscription says he crushed the 'haughty' Lakshmi-Karna, and the historian S. K. Mitra dates the decisive battle to around 1070. The Sanskrit play Prabodha-chandrodaya, staged at his court, credits the victory to a man named Gopala, perhaps a general or feudatory. Kirttivarman's gold coins may commemorate the triumph. A Persian poet records that Ibrahim of Ghazna attacked Kalanjara in these years, but there is no evidence that the fort was lost. The Chandelas were once more masters of Bundelkhand.

events.text: Madanavarman pushes west to Bhilsa on the Paramara frontier
events.detail: Madanavarman, who ruled c. 1128–1165, revived Chandela glory by subduing neighbouring kingdoms. An inscription of 1134 places him at Bhilsa (Vidisha), on the border with the Paramaras of Malwa, and he may have seized part of their territory, though the Paramaras won it back by about 1143–44. He may also have briefly occupied northern Baghelkhand while the Kalachuris were weak. His kingdom covered the Vindhyan lands between the Betwa and Yamuna rivers, and Mahoba, with its Madan Sagar lake and lakeside temples, flourished under him.

events.text: c. 1182–83: Prithviraj Chauhan defeats Paramardi and sacks Mahoba
events.detail: Paramardi (c. 1165–1203) faced the ambitious Chahamana (Chauhan) king Prithviraj III. Around 1182–83 Prithviraj invaded the Chandela kingdom and sacked Mahoba, an event confirmed by inscriptions at Madanpur. Later ballads, the source of the famous Alha-Udal legends, tell of Paramardi's generals Alha and Udal, a treacherous brother-in-law and a desperate defence, but historians doubt their details. Chandela records stay silent, probably out of shame. The blow was not fatal: Paramardi's own inscriptions from 1184 to 1201 show that he soon recovered his kingdom.

events.text: 1202–03: Qutb al-Din Aibak takes Kalanjara and Mahoba; Paramardi dies
events.detail: After the Ghurid conquest of northern India, their general Qutb al-Din Aibak, with Iltutmish, besieged Kalanjara in 1202 or 1203; the chronicles disagree on the year. According to Hasan Nizami, Paramardi agreed to become a vassal and pay tribute but died before paying; Firishta says a minister who opposed surrender killed him. His dewan, Aj Deo, held out until drought dried up the fort's reservoirs. Aibak appointed a governor at Kalanjara and also took Mahoba. The Chandelas had lost their two greatest strongholds, and their power never fully recovered.

events.text: Kalanjara, regained by Trailokyavarman, is raided by Delhi's governor of Gwalior
events.detail: Paramardi's successor Trailokyavarman (c. 1203–1245) won back much of the old domain. He took the title 'Lord of Kalanjara', suggesting that he recaptured the fortress from the Delhi Sultanate, and his coins are found across the Chandela heartland. The Persian chronicle Tabaqat-i Nasiri confirms that Kalanjara had already slipped out of Delhi's control when Iltutmish's officer Nusrat al-Din Taisi raided it in 1233. Delhi did not keep the fort, and Trailokyavarman's successors Viravarman and Bhojavarman left inscriptions at the hill fort of Ajaigarh, which became a main Chandela stronghold.

events.text: c. 1288: Hammiravarman rules without the imperial title Maharajadhiraja
events.detail: Through the 13th century the Chandelas were squeezed by the rising Muslim power of Delhi and by neighbouring dynasties. Viravarman ruled for some forty years (c. 1245–1285), followed briefly by Bhojavarman. When Hammiravarman came to the throne around 1288, he no longer used the title Maharajadhiraja, 'great king of kings', a sign of how far Chandela status had fallen. His successor Viravarman II also bore only modest titles. The main line ended around 1315, though minor branches went on ruling at Kalanjara and Mahoba; the last Kalanjara chief was killed by Sher Shah Suri's army in 1545.

name: Western Chalukya Empire (Chalukyas of Kalyani)
summary: Tailapa II seized the Rashtrakuta throne in 973 and revived the Chalukya name, ruling the western Deccan from Manyakheta and, after about 1042, from Kalyani. For a century the empire fought the Cholas over Vengi and the Tungabhadra lands, and under Vikramaditya VI (1076–1126) it stretched from the Narmada to the Kaveri country. The Kalachuris took Kalyani in 1157; Someshvara IV won it back around 1183, but the Seunas drove him into exile in 1189 and the Deccan was divided among the Hoysalas, Seunas and Kakatiyas.

events.text: Tailapa II, who overthrew the Rashtrakutas in 973, rules from Manyakheta
events.detail: Tailapa II had been a Rashtrakuta vassal governing Tardavadi, near Bijapur. When the Paramaras of Malwa sacked the Rashtrakuta capital Manyakheta in 972, he seized his chance: in 973 he overthrew Karka II and made Manyakheta his own capital. He claimed descent from the Chalukyas of Badami, a claim historians doubt. Over the next years he defeated rival claimants, won over most Rashtrakuta vassals, and sent his general Barapa to conquer Lata in southern Gujarat. His rule reached from the Narmada to the Tungabhadra.

events.text: c. 995: Tailapa captures and executes the Paramara king Munja
events.detail: The most dangerous rival in the north was Munja, king of the Paramaras of Malwa, who had inherited the power that sacked Manyakheta. The two kings fought repeatedly; according to the 14th-century writer Merutunga, Munja defeated Tailapa six times. In the end Tailapa defeated and captured Munja, and had him executed in the mid-990s. The victory secured the empire's northern frontier. Tailapa died around 997 and was succeeded by his son Satyashraya.

events.text: Rajendra Chola invades; the Chalukyas lose Gangavadi and Nolambavadi
events.detail: In the south the Chola empire of Rajaraja I was expanding fast, and Chalukya and Chola ambitions clashed over the lands along the Tungabhadra and over the Telugu kingdom of Vengi. In 1007 the Chola crown prince Rajendra invaded the Chalukya kingdom and fought Satyashraya at Donur, near Bijapur. Chola inscriptions boast of great destruction, claims that historians treat with caution. The Cholas took Gangavadi and Nolambavadi, in what is now southern Karnataka, and these lands stayed Chola for a century.

events.text: c. 1020–21: Jayasimha II fights the Cholas over the Vengi throne
events.detail: Vengi, the delta country between the Krishna and Godavari rivers, was ruled by the Eastern Chalukyas, cousins of the Western Chalukyas but allied to the Cholas by marriage. When its throne fell vacant around 1020, the Western Chalukya king Jayasimha II (1015–1042) backed one claimant and the Chola emperor Rajendra I another. The quarrel over Vengi became the central cause of half a century of Chalukya–Chola warfare. Around 1024 Jayasimha also subdued the Paramaras and the rebellious Yadava king Bhillama in the north.

events.text: c. 1042: Someshvara I moves the capital to Kalyani
events.detail: Jayasimha's son Someshvara I (1042–1068) was an energetic soldier who as a prince had led raids as far as Bihar and Bengal. Around 1042 he moved the capital from Manyakheta to Kalyani (modern Basavakalyan, in northern Karnataka), which gave the dynasty its other name, the Chalukyas of Kalyani. Kalyani grew into a splendid royal city and centre of Kannada and Sanskrit learning. From here Someshvara renewed the wars with the Cholas on the Tungabhadra and in Vengi.

events.text: Battle of Koppam: Someshvara I routed, but the Chola king is killed
events.detail: The Chalukya–Chola wars reached a bloody climax at Koppam, on 'the Great River', probably the Krishna, on 28 May 1052 (some date it 1054). The Chola emperor Rajadhiraja I and his brother Rajendra II met Someshvara I's army. Rajadhiraja, riding an elephant, was mortally wounded by Chalukya archers, but Rajendra rallied the Chola troops, crowned himself on the battlefield and routed the Chalukyas; Someshvara fled. Neither side could win outright, and the long war along the Krishna–Tungabhadra frontier went on.

events.text: Defeat at Vijayawada; Vengi lost, Someshvara I drowns himself
events.detail: In 1066 the Chalukya prince Vikramaditya raided deep into Chola country, but the Cholas struck back. In 1068 the Chola emperor Virarajendra defeated Someshvara I near Vijayawada, and the Chalukyas lost their hold on Vengi. Soon afterwards Someshvara, suffering from an incurable illness, drowned himself in the Tungabhadra river in a ritual suicide. His eldest son Someshvara II succeeded him but quarrelled with his ambitious younger brother Vikramaditya, and civil war followed.

events.text: Vikramaditya VI deposes his brother and starts the Chalukya-Vikrama era
events.detail: Vikramaditya VI, backed by the Chola king Virarajendra and by powerful vassals such as the Hoysalas, Seunas and Kadambas of Hangal, defeated his brother Someshvara II and took him captive. He was crowned on 11 February 1076 and launched a new calendar, the Chalukya-Vikrama era, replacing the Shaka era in his records. His fifty-year reign was the empire's golden age. The Kashmiri poet Bilhana wrote his life, the Vikramankadevacharita, and the jurist Vijnaneshwara wrote the Mitakshara, a lasting work of Hindu law, at his court.

events.text: Vikramaditya VI takes Kanchipuram from the Cholas
events.detail: Vikramaditya VI kept up the pressure on the Cholas, now ruled by Kulottunga I. In 1085 he invaded the Tamil country and captured Kanchipuram, the old Pallava capital, and in 1088 he conquered parts of Vengi. In the north he subdued the Shilaharas of the Konkan and the Seunas of Devagiri, raided Lata (Gujarat) and checked the Kalachuris of Ratanpur. At its height the empire ran from the Narmada river in the north to the Tumkur and Cuddapah regions in the south, and east to the Godavari districts.

events.text: General Anantapala wins Vengi back from the Cholas
events.detail: Vengi had changed hands several times: Vikramaditya held it from 1093 until the Cholas retook it in 1099. Late in the reign of the Chola king Kulottunga I, the Chalukyas struck again, and in 1118 their general Anantapala took Vengi and governed it for the emperor. At the same time the Hoysalas took Gangavadi from the Cholas. Vengi stayed Chalukya until about 1124, but after Vikramaditya's death in 1126 the Chola king Vikrama Chola recovered it by 1133.

events.text: Someshvara III compiles the Manasollasa, an encyclopedia of royal life
events.detail: Vikramaditya VI's son Someshvara III (1126–1138) was more scholar than soldier. In 1129 he completed the Manasollasa, a Sanskrit encyclopedia covering government, warfare, medicine, architecture, cooking, music, sport and the pleasures of kingship. It is a priceless picture of court life in medieval India. But his reign also saw losses: Vengi slipped back to the Cholas, and the great vassal families, the Hoysalas of the south, the Kakatiyas of Telangana and the Seunas of the north, grew steadily more independent.

events.text: The Kalachuri Bijjala II seizes Kalyani; the court flees to Annigeri
events.detail: By the mid-12th century the empire was falling apart. In 1149 the Kakatiya king Prola defeated and captured Tailapa III, a blow to Chalukya prestige. The Kalachuri Bijjala II, a powerful vassal in the north-west, then turned on his overlords and in 1157 took Kalyani. The Chalukya court withdrew south to Annigeri, and the Kalachuris ruled the capital for about twenty years. The empire was reduced to a shadow, while the Hoysalas, Seunas and Kakatiyas acted as independent kings.

events.text: c. 1183: Someshvara IV recovers Kalyani in a last Chalukya revival
events.detail: When Kalachuri power weakened, Someshvara IV made a final bid to restore the dynasty. Around 1183 he recaptured Kalyani; his general Narasimha killed the Kalachuri king Sankama, and another general, Barma, defeated the Seunas. The revival was brief. The Hoysala king Veera Ballala II defeated Someshvara and the Seuna Bhillama V in the Krishna valley, and in 1189 the Seunas drove Someshvara into exile at Banavasi. The Chalukya empire was divided among the Seunas, Hoysalas and Kakatiyas.

name: Paramara dynasty of Malwa
summary: The Paramaras, a Rajput dynasty of Malwa, broke free of their Rashtrakuta overlords when Siyaka II sacked Manyakheta in 972, and ruled from Dhara. Munja and the scholar-king Bhoja (c. 1010–1055) made Malwa a great power and a centre of learning, but Chalukya, Kalachuri and Gujarati attacks wore it down, and from c. 1136 to c. 1175 Malwa was held by the Chaulukyas of Gujarat. Vindhyavarman restored the kingdom, which survived raids from Gujarat, the Deccan and Delhi until Alauddin Khalji's general killed the last king, Mahalakadeva, in 1305.

events.text: Munja (r. c. 972–994) sacks Aghata and wins Chittor from the Guhilas of Mewar
events.detail: Siyaka II had made the Paramaras independent of the Rashtrakutas by sacking their capital, Manyakheta, in 972. His son Vakpati Munja, king from about 972, turned this freedom into conquest. He plundered Aghata, the capital of the Guhilas of Mewar, and the Paramaras gained eastern Mewar, including the great fort of Chittor. He also claimed victories over the Kalachuris of Tripuri, the Chahamanas, the Hunas and a Chalukya ruler of Lata, though some of these brought no new land. Munja, a poet and a patron of poets, is credited with the Munja Sagar lake at Dhar.

events.text: Between 994 and 998: Munja is captured and executed by the Chalukya Tailapa II
events.detail: Munja's most dangerous rival was Tailapa II, founder of the Western Chalukya kingdom in the Deccan. The 14th-century writer Merutunga claims Munja beat Tailapa six times. Ignoring his minister's advice, Munja then crossed the Godavari to finish him off, but his army was defeated and he was taken prisoner and executed. The date falls between 994, when a text describes him as still reigning, and Tailapa's death in 998. The Chalukyas seized the southern part of the Paramara kingdom, possibly as far as the Narmada river.

events.text: c. 1000: Sindhuraja defeats the Chalukya Satyashraya and recovers lost lands
events.detail: Munja was succeeded by his brother Sindhuraja, not by Bhoja as later legend claimed. Sindhuraja defeated Satyashraya of the Western Chalukyas and won back the territory lost in the Deccan war. He also campaigned against the Hunas, the Somavanshis of south Kosala, the Shilaharas of the Konkan and the ruler of Lata. His court poet Padmagupta celebrated these wars in the Nava-sahasanka-charita, which also first records the legend that the Paramaras were born from a sacred fire. Historians think the poem exaggerates, but Sindhuraja left Malwa strong for his son Bhoja.

events.text: Bhoja becomes king of Malwa, ruling from Dhara
events.detail: Bhoja, the most famous Paramara king, came to the throne around 1010; his earliest record, the Modasa copper plates, dates from 1010–11. Ruling from Dhara (modern Dhar), he was celebrated as a scholar-king and patron of learning. He founded the Bhojshala, a centre of Sanskrit study with a temple of Sarasvati, and is credited with founding Bhojpur, where dams held back a great lake around the Bhojeshwar Temple. Under him Dhara and Malwa became leading centres of learning, and his long reign, to about 1055, was the high point of Paramara power.

events.text: c. 1018: Bhoja conquers Lata and, by 1020, the northern Konkan
events.detail: Bhoja spent much of his reign at war. Around 1018 he invaded Lata, in what is now southern Gujarat, and subjugated its Chalukya rulers. Between 1018 and 1020 he also captured the Konkan coast from the Shilaharas and celebrated with a victory festival. He joined Rajendra Chola and the Kalachuri Gangeya in an alliance against the Western Chalukya king Jayasimha II, a war in which both sides claimed victory. At its height his kingdom stretched from Chittor in the north to the upper Konkan in the south, and from the Sabarmati river in the west to Vidisha in the east.

events.text: After 1042: the Chalukya Someshvara I sacks Dhara; the southern frontier falls back
events.detail: The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani remained Bhoja's great enemy. Some time after 1042 their king Someshvara I invaded Malwa and sacked Dhara, and later Chalukya inscriptions boast of plundering Dhara, Ujjain and Mandu. Bhoja recovered his capital and his kingdom, but the war cost him his southern lands: the Konkan was lost, and the Paramara frontier moved back from the Godavari to the Narmada. Bhoja also failed against the Kachchhapaghatas of Gwalior and was checked by the Chandelas in the east, so his kingdom stopped growing.

events.text: c. 1055: Bhoja dies as Gujarat and the Kalachuris invade Malwa
events.detail: Near the end of Bhoja's reign two neighbours joined forces against him: the Chaulukya king Bhima I of Gujarat and the Kalachuri king Karna. According to Merutunga, Bhoja refused to accept Karna's overlordship and died of disease just as the allied armies attacked, in about 1055. His successor Jayasimha I faced the invasion and may have needed help from the Chalukyas of Kalyani, his father's old enemies, to survive. Bhoja's empire did not outlive him: from now on the Paramaras were mostly defending Malwa rather than expanding it.

events.text: Udayaditya takes the throne and drives back a Chaulukya invasion
events.detail: Bhoja's brother Udayaditya came to the throne around 1070. He repulsed a Chaulukya invasion from Gujarat under Karna, but he was also defeated by his own vassal Chamundaraja of Vagada, a sign that control over the outer Paramara lands was slipping. His successor Lakshmadeva (c. 1086–1094) was later credited with sweeping conquests in a court eulogy, but historians think these were exaggerated; at most he defeated the Kalachuris of Tripuri. The kingdom held together, but rival powers pressed on it from every side.

events.text: c. 1135–36: Jayasimha Siddharaja of Gujarat takes Dhara and jails the Paramara king
events.detail: Under Naravarman (c. 1094–1133) the Paramaras lost wars to the Chandelas and to Jayasimha Siddharaja, the Chaulukya king of Gujarat. The war with Gujarat ended under Yashovarman, when Jayasimha, helped by Chahamana allies, captured Dhara; the historian A. K. Majumdar dates this to about 1135–36. Gujarati writers say the Malwa king was carried off in a cage, though the sources disagree on whether he was Naravarman or Yashovarman. By 1137 Jayasimha was calling himself Avantinatha, 'Lord of Avanti', and he set a governor over Ujjain. Malwa had become part of the Chaulukya realm.

events.text: c. 1150: Kumarapala defeats the usurper Ballala; Malwa becomes a Gujarat province
events.detail: Paramara rule did not vanish at once. After Jayasimha's death, Jayavarman I took the royal title and briefly regained Dhara around 1142–43, but he lost it to a usurper named Ballala. Around 1150 the new Chaulukya king Kumarapala defeated Ballala with help from the Chahamana ruler Alhana of Naddula and the Paramara chief of Abu. Malwa was now a province of Gujarat, and for about a generation the main Paramara line had no kingdom. A junior Paramara branch, the Mahakumaras, kept some lands around Bhopal.

events.text: c. 1175: Vindhyavarman defeats Gujarat and restores the Paramara kingdom
events.detail: Around 1175 Jayavarman's son Vindhyavarman defeated the king of Gujarat and re-established Paramara rule in Malwa, according to an inscription of his grandson Arjunavarman. Historians disagree about whether his opponent was the Chaulukya Mularaja II. His position was never secure: the Hoysalas and the Yadavas of Devagiri invaded from the south, and the Chaulukya general Kumara defeated him at Goggasthana. Even so, he had regained the capital, Dhara, by 1192. His son Subhatavarman, who succeeded in 1194, was strong enough to raid Gujarat in turn.

events.text: c. 1234: Sultan Iltutmish's army sacks Bhilsa and raids Ujjain
events.detail: By the 13th century the Delhi Sultanate had become the strongest power in northern India. In 1233–35 (the sources differ) Sultan Iltutmish raided the Paramara cities of Bhilsa (Vidisha) and Ujjain. At Bhilsa his army occupied the city and destroyed a great temple, and at Ujjain it damaged the Mahakaleshwar temple and carried off rich plunder. Iltutmish made little effort to annex Malwa, and the Paramara king Devapala soon recaptured Bhilsa. But the raid exposed the kingdom's weakness. Squeezed by Delhi, Gujarat and the Yadavas, it lasted until 1305, when Alauddin Khalji's general killed the last king.

reigns.name: Interregnum: Ballala, then Chaulukya rule from Gujarat

name: Eastern Ganga dynasty
summary: The Eastern Gangas had ruled a small kingdom in southern Kalinga from Kalinganagara since about 500, and in the 11th century Vajrahasta V and Rajaraja I turned it into a regional power. Anantavarman Chodaganga (1078–1150) conquered Utkala, ruled from the Ganges to the Godavari and began the Jagannath temple at Puri. His successors held off the Muslim rulers of Bengal, and Narasimhadeva I (1238–1264) struck at Lakhnauti and built the Sun Temple at Konark, but the dynasty declined after him and was ended by the usurper Kapilendra in 1434.

events.text: Vajrahasta V, 'lord of the three Kalingas', rules from Kalinganagara
events.detail: The Eastern Gangas, probably an offshoot of the Western Gangas of Karnataka, had ruled part of Kalinga, on India's east coast, since about 500, with their capital at Kalinganagara (Mukhalingam). For centuries they were a minor dynasty, often under stronger neighbours. Vajrahasta V, king from 1038 to about 1070, revived their fortunes. He took the grand titles Trikalingadhipati and Sakalakalingadhipati, 'lord of the three Kalingas' and 'lord of all Kalinga', challenged the Somavamshi kings to the north and allied with the Kalachuris.

events.text: c. 1070: Rajaraja Deva I defeats the Somavamshis and weds a Chola princess
events.detail: Vajrahasta's son Rajaraja Deva I (c. 1070–1077) pushed Ganga power further. He defeated the Somavamshi king of Utkala to the north and extended his authority towards the Vengi region to the south. His relations with the mighty Chola empire mixed war and diplomacy: he married a Chola princess, Rajasundari, a daughter of the emperor Virarajendra. Their son, half Ganga and half Chola, would become the greatest king of the dynasty, Anantavarman Chodaganga, whose name joins both lines.

events.text: Anantavarman Chodaganga begins a 72-year reign
events.detail: Anantavarman Chodaganga succeeded his father on 17 February 1078 (some lists say 1077), and by his own inscription he reigned for 72 years. In his early years the Cholas attacked and for a time took the Visakhapatnam district, but he recovered his lands. He then turned to expansion. Over the following decades he made the Gangas the dominant power of the eastern coast, ruling from the Godavari in the south to Midnapore in Bengal in the north, between the Bay of Bengal and the Eastern Ghats.

events.text: c. 1112: Chodaganga conquers Utkala and moves the capital to Cuttack
events.detail: North of Kalinga lay Utkala, the heart of modern Odisha, ruled by the Somavamshi (Kesari) kings. According to the Madalapanji, the chronicle of the Puri temple, Chodaganga defeated the last Kesari king and moved his capital to Chaudwar-Cuttack on the Mahanadi. The conquest is dated to about 1112, and a grant of 1118 claims sovereignty over all of Utkala. It united Kalinga and Utkala into a single kingdom, roughly the Odisha of later history, and shifted the dynasty's centre north from Kalinganagara.

events.text: c. 1135: Building of the great Jagannath temple at Puri begins
events.detail: Chodaganga, a Shaiva by birth, turned to Vaishnavism, reportedly under the influence of the teacher Ramanuja. He began the present temple of Jagannath, a form of Vishnu, at Puri on the coast of Utkala. Its start is not dated exactly: an inscription of 1134–1135 records his donation, so building probably began between 1112 and the 1130s, and it was completed around 1150–1161. The temple became the religious heart of the kingdom and one of the holiest pilgrimage sites in India, famous for its Ratha Yatra chariot festival.

events.text: Chodaganga dies, leaving an empire from the Ganges to the Godavari
events.detail: Late in his reign Chodaganga attacked Bengal after the death of the Pala king Ramapala, defeated the king of Mandara and destroyed the fortified town of Aramya, possibly Arambagh in Hooghly. He also took the part of Vengi north of the Godavari. He died around 1150 (some sources say 1147), and his kingdom was described as reaching from the Ganges to the Godavari. His successors, Kamarnava, Raghava, Rajaraja II and Anangabhima II, ruled quietly for half a century, though Kamarnava failed to win Sambalpur from the Kalachuris of Ratanpur.

events.text: Muslim rulers of Bengal reach the frontier; first incursion turns back
events.detail: At the start of the 13th century Turkish commanders from north India conquered western Bengal and made Lakhnauti their capital, bringing Muslim rule to the Ganga kingdom's northern border. In 1205, in the reign of Rajaraja Deva III, Muhammad Sheran Khalji advanced towards Lakhnauti in what was the first Muslim incursion threatening the kingdom, but he withdrew without invading Odisha. For the rest of the dynasty's history, the Bengal frontier was its most dangerous border, and the Ganga kings had to defend their kingdom against repeated attacks from the north.

events.text: Anangabhima III takes the throne and makes Jagannath the state deity
events.detail: Anangabhima Deva III (1211–1238) ruled from the Ganga river to the Godavari. With his general and minister Vishnu he beat back invasions by Ghiyasuddin Iwaz Shah, the ruler of Bengal. He defeated the Kalachuris of Ratanpur and took the Sambalpur–Bolangir region. He founded a new capital at Cuttack, at the meeting of the Mahanadi and Kathajodi rivers, with the Barabati fort. He also dedicated his kingdom to Jagannath and called himself the god's deputy, making the deity of Puri the divine sovereign of Odisha.

events.text: c. 1230s: The Kakatiyas push north across the Godavari delta
events.detail: In the south the Kakatiya kings of Telangana were expanding. In the 1230s the Kakatiya ruler Ganapati Deva brought the Godavari and Krishna deltas under his control, and his power reached into the Ganjam district of southern Odisha. Anangabhima III fought the Kakatiyas, but they took territory up to the East Godavari region. The southern frontier, which under Chodaganga had lain on the Godavari, was pushed back, and the Telugu coastal lands were lost to the Gangas.

events.text: Narasimhadeva I invades Bengal and wins at Katasin
events.detail: Anangabhima's son Narasimhadeva I (1238–1264) chose to attack rather than wait. In 1242–1243 his army marched against Tughral Tughan Khan, the Delhi Sultanate's governor of Bengal, and took control of Rarh, west of the Hooghly. When Tughan counter-attacked, the Odia forces met him near Katasin (Contai) with trenches, hidden troops and a feigned retreat, and a surprise attack inflicted heavy losses; Tughan narrowly escaped. It was one of the few defeats inflicted on the Bengal sultanate's armies in that era.

events.text: Narasimhadeva's army besieges Lakhnauti, capital of Muslim Bengal
events.detail: Following up his victory, Narasimhadeva sent his army deep into Bengal in 1244. It took two provinces and surrounded the fort of Lakhnauti, the capital, and the Muslim commander Fakhr-ul-Mulk Karimuddin Laghri was killed. Tughan Khan appealed to Delhi, and the governor of Awadh, Tamur Khan, arrived with reinforcements, so the siege was short. Tughan was removed and Tamur took over Bengal. Narasimhadeva's campaign kept the Muslim rulers of Bengal on the defensive and secured Odisha's northern frontier for decades.

events.text: c. 1250: Narasimhadeva I, the first 'Gajapati', builds the Sun Temple at Konark
events.detail: In a 1246 inscription Narasimhadeva became the first Odisha king to use the title Gajapati, 'lord of elephants', which later rulers of Odisha kept for centuries. Around 1250 he built the great temple of Surya, the sun god, at Konark on the coast, reportedly to celebrate his victories over Bengal. It was designed as a colossal stone chariot pulled by seven horses on 24 carved wheels. Its main tower, once over 60 metres high, has collapsed, but the temple is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and a masterpiece of Odisha's architecture.

events.text: Death of Narasimhadeva I; the long Ganga decline begins
events.detail: Narasimhadeva I died in 1264, and with him ended the dynasty's age of conquest. His successors, Bhanu Deva I, Narasimha Deva II, Bhanu Deva II and Narasimha Deva III, held Odisha for almost another century, but they were mostly on the defensive against the Delhi Sultanate, its governors in Bengal and the powers of the south. In the 1350s Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq invaded and levied tribute. The last king, Bhanu Deva IV, was overthrown in 1434–35 by his minister Kapilendra, founder of the Gajapati dynasty.

name: Sena dynasty of Bengal
summary: The Senas, a family from Karnataka settled in Rarh in western Bengal, served the Palas until Vijaya Sena (1096–1159) won independence and drove the last Pala king out of Gauda. Under Ballala Sena and Lakshmana Sena they ruled almost all of Bengal and patronised Sanskrit learning. In 1203–04 Bakhtiyar Khalji's horsemen surprised the old king at Nadia; the Senas lost western and northern Bengal and held out in the east until about 1230.

events.text: c. 1072: Samanta Sena, a migrant from Karnataka, founds the line in Rarh
events.detail: The Sena family came from the Kannada-speaking south. Their own Deopara inscription describes the founder, Samanta Sena, as a Brahmakshatriya, a Brahmin family that had taken up the warrior's role, who had migrated from Karnataka. He settled in Rarh, in western Bengal, and is dated about 1070 to 1095. At first the family held a subordinate position under the Pala kings, who were then struggling with rebellion in their heartland of Varendra.

events.text: Hemanta Sena declares himself king
events.detail: Samanta Sena's son Hemanta Sena took the next step. In 1095 he usurped power and styled himself king, ruling for about a year until 1096. The Pala kingdom was weak: Ramapala had only just recovered Varendra from the Kaivarta rebels and depended on the loyalty of local chiefs. Families such as the Senas could bargain their support for more freedom, and Hemanta's claim to royal status marked the Senas' rise from local lords to a ruling dynasty.

events.text: Vijaya Sena begins a reign of over sixty years
events.detail: Hemanta's son Vijaya Sena succeeded in 1096 and ruled for about 62 years, until 1159. He inherited a subordinate position in Rarh under the Palas but won his independence in return for helping Ramapala. His marriage to a princess of the Sura family strengthened his hold on Rarh, and he was remembered as a friend of the Eastern Ganga king Anantavarman Chodaganga of Odisha. Patiently, he turned a western Bengal lordship into a kingdom ready to challenge the Palas themselves.

events.text: c. 1153: Vijaya Sena defeats Madanapala and takes the throne of Gauda
events.detail: Pala records run to Madanapala's eighth regnal year, 1152–53. Most probably soon afterwards, Vijaya Sena defeated him, and the Pala king fled; Vijaya Sena then took the throne of Gauda. His Deopara inscription, near Rajshahi, lists victories over Nanya of Mithila, Raghava, probably the Eastern Ganga king of Odisha, and others, and says his fleet sailed west up the Ganges. He ruled from Vijayapuri and Bikrampur (Vikramapura), and Bengal was now united under the Senas.

events.text: Ballala Sena succeeds and ends the last Pala resistance
events.detail: Vijaya Sena's son Ballala Sena ruled from about 1159 to 1179. He is credited with defeating Govindapala and so ending the Pala dynasty, and he may have completed the conquest of northern Bengal and taken Magadha and Mithila. Tradition gives his kingdom five provinces: Vanga, Varendra, Rarh, Mithila and Bagari. He married Ramadevi, a Western Chalukya princess from the Deccan. Later tradition links him to the system of Kulinism among Brahmins and Kayasthas, but historians doubt this.

events.text: Ballala Sena completes the Danasagara, a Sanskrit work on gift-giving
events.detail: The Sena kings presented themselves as champions of Brahminical Hinduism and Sanskrit learning, in contrast to the Buddhist Palas. Ballala Sena was himself an author. According to a Sena inscription he wrote the Danasagara, a treatise on religious gift-giving, in 1168, and in 1169 he began the Adbhutasagara, a work on omens, which was left unfinished. In old age he and his queen reportedly retired to the confluence of the Ganges and Yamuna, leaving his son Lakshmana Sena in charge.

events.text: Lakshmana Sena becomes king; his armies claim victories to Varanasi
events.detail: Lakshmana Sena had fought for his grandfather and father against Gauda, Kamarupa, Kalinga and the Gahadavala king Jayachandra of Varanasi. As king from about 1179 to 1206 he carried the Sena kingdom into Odisha and possibly as far as Varanasi; a later Sena inscription credits him with victory pillars at Varanasi, Allahabad and on the southern seacoast. His court included the poets Jayadeva, Dhoyi and Sharana and the scholar Halayudha, and his era was used to date documents in Bengal and Bihar for centuries.

events.text: Bakhtiyar Khalji's raiders overrun Bihar and its monasteries
events.detail: After the Ghurid victories in northern India, the Turkic commander Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji began raiding east of Varanasi in the late 1190s. By 1200 he had subjugated much of Bihar, the old Pala heartland west of the Sena kingdom. His attacks destroyed the Buddhist monastic universities of Odantapuri and Vikramashila, according to later accounts, though whether he also destroyed Nalanda is debated. With Bihar in Muslim hands, the road into Bengal lay open.

events.text: c. 1204: Bakhtiyar surprises Nadia; the old king Lakshmana Sena flees
events.detail: Having taken Bihar, Bakhtiyar Khalji struck at Nadia (Nabadwip), where the aged Lakshmana Sena was staying, in 1203–04. The fullest account, in the Tabaqat-i-Nasiri written by 1260, says he arrived with a band of horsemen and was at first taken for a horse dealer; it is said only 18 riders kept up with his rapid advance. The old king, surprised at his dinner, fled with his retainers to eastern Bengal. Nadia fell, and the Senas lost western Bengal almost without a battle.

events.text: c. 1205: Bakhtiyar makes Lakhnauti (Gaur) his capital; north Bengal is lost
events.detail: Rather than stay at Nadia, Bakhtiyar Khalji moved north to Lakhnauti, the old capital of Gauda, and made it the seat of his government; the Ghurid conquest of Bengal is usually dated to 1205. Northern Bengal (Varendra) came under his rule. The Senas kept only the south and east, the region of Vanga, ruled from Bikrampur near modern Dhaka. Bengal was now divided between a Muslim state in the northwest and a Hindu Sena kingdom in the east.

events.text: Lakshmana Sena dies; his son Vishvarupa Sena rules eastern Bengal
events.detail: Lakshmana Sena died around 1206, the same year Bakhtiyar Khalji was assassinated after a disastrous campaign toward Tibet. Lakshmana's sons continued Sena rule in southeastern Bengal, out of reach of the new Muslim rulers in the northwest. Vishvarupa Sena reigned from about 1206 to 1225, keeping the dynasty independent in the south and east of Bengal, far from Lakhnauti. Bikrampur, already a Sena capital, became the centre of the shrunken kingdom in the Ganges delta.

events.text: Keshava Sena succeeds his brother Vishvarupa
events.detail: Keshava Sena, another son of Lakshmana Sena, followed Vishvarupa Sena around 1225 and reigned until about 1230. Like his brother he kept the Sena kingdom independent in southern and eastern Bengal. His copper-plate inscription is a key source: it credits his father and grandfather with victory pillars at Varanasi, Allahabad and the southern sea, recalling the dynasty's days of glory. The kingdom he ruled, however, was only the eastern part of the Bengal his family once held.

events.text: c. 1230: Sena rule fades; the Deva dynasty rises in eastern Bengal
events.detail: The Sena dynasty is usually said to end around 1230, after Keshava Sena. The Persian chronicle Tabaqat-i-Nasiri suggests that descendants of Lakshmana Sena still ruled somewhere in eastern Bengal as late as 1245 or even 1260. In the southeast a new Hindu family, the Deva dynasty, rose to power; its strongest king, Damodaradeva, ruled from about 1231 to 1243 around Comilla, Noakhali and Chittagong, and a later king took Bikrampur.

name: Hoysala Empire
summary: The Hoysalas, hill chiefs of the Malnad in southern Karnataka, became a regional power when Vishnuvardhana drove the Cholas out of Gangavadi around 1116. Veera Ballala II threw off Chalukya overlordship around 1192, and his successors ruled the Kannada country and much of the Kaveri valley, with a second capital near Srirangam. Delhi armies sacked their capital Halebidu in 1311 and again around 1327; Veera Ballala III died fighting the Sultan of Madurai in 1343, and by 1346 the kingdom had passed to the new Vijayanagara state.

events.text: c. 1116: Vishnuvardhana defeats the Cholas at Talakad and takes Gangavadi
events.detail: In the early 12th century the Hoysalas were a hill family of the Malnad region, nominally serving the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani. The Cholas held Gangavadi, the plateau around Talakad on the Kaveri, in what is now southern Karnataka. Vishnuvardhana, king from 1108, made its conquest his first great goal. His forces defeated the Chola general Adiyamma near Talakad, in 1116 according to the Hoysala Empire article, and Vishnuvardhana took the title Talakadugonda, 'conqueror of Talakad'. With Gangavadi in hand, the Hoysalas ruled the whole southern Karnataka plateau.

events.text: Chennakesava temple at Belur celebrates the victory over the Cholas
events.detail: Vishnuvardhana had been born a Jain, but under the influence of the philosopher Ramanuja he came to support Vaishnavism, while his queen Shantala Devi and others in his family stayed Jain. To celebrate his success against the Cholas he built the Chennakesava temple at Belur, dedicated to Vishnu and dated to 1117 in the Hoysala Empire article. Its richly carved stone set the style now called Hoysala architecture, and the Hoysaleswara temple at the royal capital, Halebidu, followed around 1121. These temples showed that the Hoysalas were no longer minor chiefs but kings with imperial ambitions.

events.text: c. 1140: Hoysalas recover Hangal, Uchchangi and Bankapura in the north
events.detail: Vishnuvardhana also tried to break free of his overlord, the Chalukya emperor Vikramaditya VI. His armies met Chalukya forces at Kannegala around 1118, but around 1122 he was defeated by the Sinda chief Achugi, a Chalukya commander, and had to accept Chalukya overlordship for a time. After Vikramaditya VI died, Chalukya power weakened. By about 1140 Vishnuvardhana had recaptured Hangal, Uchchangi and Bankapura, strongholds in what is now northern Karnataka. The Hoysala kingdom was pushing north toward the Tungabhadra, into the old Chalukya heartland.

events.text: c. 1191: Veera Ballala II defeats the Yadavas at Soratur and Lakkundi
events.detail: As the Chalukya empire collapsed in the 1180s, the Hoysalas and the Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri raced to take its lands. Around 1187-1189 the Yadava king Bhillama V seized the old Chalukya capital, Kalyani. Veera Ballala II, Hoysala king from 1173, marched north and defeated Bhillama's army at Soratur and Lakkundi, in present-day Gadag district, around 1191 (the Seuna dynasty article places the battle in the late 1180s). The Yadavas were pushed back beyond the Malaprabha and Krishna rivers, which became the Hoysala-Yadava border for about two decades.

events.text: c. 1192: Ballala II crowns himself; the Hoysalas become fully independent
events.detail: With the Chalukyas gone and the Yadavas beaten back, Veera Ballala II no longer needed to acknowledge any overlord. Around 1192 he crowned himself emperor over the Karnataka region; the Hoysala Empire article dates the declaration of independence to 1193. He ruled from Halebidu (Dwarasamudra), where the Kedareshwara temple was built in his reign, and he patronised Kannada poets such as Janna and Rudrabhatta. For a while, in one historian's phrase, the Hoysalas were paramount throughout most of the Kannada-speaking Deccan, from the Kaveri valley north to the Krishna.

events.text: c. 1212: The Yadava king Simhana takes the lands north of the Tungabhadra
events.detail: The northern border did not hold. The Yadava king Simhana II, the greatest ruler of his dynasty, attacked while the Hoysalas were busy with wars in the Tamil south. Yadava inscriptions appear south of the Malaprabha from 1202, and by 1213 they had annexed most of present-day Dharwad district. Banavasi fell before 1215, and by 1220 the whole area north of the Tungabhadra was in Yadava hands; the article on Ballala II dates the main loss to after about 1212. The Hoysala kingdom shrank back toward the southern plateau, and its kings turned their ambitions south instead.

events.text: c. 1217: Hoysalas restore the Chola king; Ballala II hailed 'emperor of the south'
events.detail: Around 1216 the Pandya king Maravarman Sundara Pandya invaded the Chola kingdom and drove King Kulothunga III into exile. The Chola king asked the Hoysalas for help. Ballala II sent an army under his son, the future Narasimha II, which repulsed the Pandyas and put Kulothunga back on his throne. Ballala took titles such as Cholarajyapratishtacharya, 'establisher of the Chola kingdom', and Dakshina Chakravarti, 'emperor of the south', and gained direct control of parts of the Kaveri plains around Srirangam. From now on the Hoysalas were arbiters of Tamil politics.

events.text: c. 1236: Vira Someshwara rules from a second capital at Kannanur near Srirangam
events.detail: Under Narasimha II and his son Vira Someshwara the Hoysalas played the Cholas and Pandyas against each other. The Hoysala Empire article says Kannanur Kuppam, near Srirangam, became a provincial capital around 1225; the article on Someshwara says he founded his capital there after 1235 and named it Vikramapura. He conquered Magadai Mandalam in 1236 and switched sides between the Tamil kings as it suited him, and they called him 'Mamadi', uncle. With a royal seat on the Kaveri, the Hoysala realm stretched from the Western Ghats deep into Tamil country.

events.text: Someshwara divides the kingdom between his sons Narasimha III and Ramanatha
events.detail: In 1254 Vira Someshwara split his kingdom between two sons. Narasimha III ruled the Karnataka heartland from Halebidu, while Ramanatha ruled the Tamil possessions from Kannanur. Someshwara himself stayed at Kannanur with Ramanatha and was later killed in a war with the Pandya king Sadayavarman Sundara Pandyan I, who was building a new Pandya empire. The division weakened the dynasty at a dangerous moment. Hoysala dominance in the south, strongest between about 1220 and 1245, faded as the Pandyas rose, and the kingdom was increasingly confined to the Karnataka plateau.

events.text: Malik Kafur's Delhi army sacks Halebidu; Ballala III pays tribute
events.detail: Veera Ballala III, king from 1292, recovered some lost Tamil territory and fought off the Yadavas, defeating them at Holalkere around 1305. But a new power had reached the Deccan: the Delhi Sultanate. After subduing Devagiri and Warangal, Sultan Alauddin Khalji sent his general Malik Kafur south. His army besieged the Hoysala capital, Halebidu, from 25 February 1311. Ballala accepted defeat, handed over great wealth, agreed to pay annual tribute and sent his son to Delhi. Kafur then pushed on to plunder the Pandya kingdom. The Hoysalas survived, but as tributaries of Delhi.

events.text: c. 1327: A Tughluq army sacks Halebidu again; Ballala III moves to Tiruvannamalai
events.detail: In the 1320s the Tughluq sultans of Delhi annexed the Deccan kingdoms one by one: Warangal fell in 1323 and the small Kampili kingdom on the Tungabhadra around 1327-1328. Around 1327 a Tughluq army sacked Halebidu for a second time. Ballala III retreated to Tiruvannamalai, in the Tamil country, and kept up the resistance from there. By about 1336 every other Hindu kingdom of the south had fallen, and the Hoysala king was the last of the old dynasties still standing. Two officers who had served him, Harihara and Bukka, now administered his northern lands.

events.text: Ballala III is captured and killed fighting the Sultan of Madurai
events.detail: In 1335 the Delhi governor of Madurai, Jalaluddin Ahsan Khan, declared an independent Madurai Sultanate in the far south. The aged Ballala III made war on it. Around 1342-1343 he fought Sultan Ghiyas-ud-Din Damghani at Kannanur Koppam, near Srirangam, and came close to victory, but he was captured and killed; the Madurai Sultanate article says his body was displayed on the walls of Madurai. Some sources date his death to 8 September 1342, others to 1343. With the king gone, Hoysala resistance collapsed.

events.text: The Hoysala kingdom ends; its lands pass to the new Vijayanagara state
events.detail: Ballala III's son, Veera Ballala IV, held the title for a few years, but he is said to have met a similar end around 1346. In the north, Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family, who had served the Hoysala king as commanders, had been administering Hoysala territory since about 1336 and had founded a new state at Vijayanagara. By 1346 the Hoysala kingdom was gone, merged into the Vijayanagara realm. That year Queen Krishnayitayi and Harihara I made grants to the Sringeri monastery on the same day, a sign of the handover. The Hoysala heartland became the core of the new empire.

name: Kakatiya dynasty
summary: The Kakatiyas, long-time vassals of the Chalukyas of Kalyani, declared independence under Rudradeva around 1163 and made Orugallu (Warangal) their capital. Ganapati (c. 1199–1262) brought almost all the Telugu-speaking lands, from the Telangana uplands to the Godavari–Krishna delta, under one rule, and his daughter Rudrama Devi governed as one of India's few reigning queens. Delhi armies made Prataparudra II a tributary in 1310, and in 1323 the future Muhammad bin Tughluq took Warangal and ended the dynasty.

events.text: c. 1195: Rudradeva dies; Orugallu (Warangal) becomes the Kakatiya capital
events.detail: The Kakatiyas had served the Chalukyas of Kalyani for generations from their fief at Anumakonda (Hanamkonda) in Telangana. As Chalukya power faded, Rudradeva subdued rival chiefs and, around 1163, proclaimed himself a sovereign king; from then on Kakatiya inscriptions used Telugu rather than Kannada. He built the Thousand Pillar Temple at Anumakonda and began moving the capital to nearby Orugallu, modern Warangal, which the Kakatiya dynasty article dates to 1195. Rudradeva died around 1195, perhaps killed fighting the Yadava king Jaitugi, though historians dispute this. His brother Mahadeva succeeded him.

events.text: Mahadeva is killed fighting the Yadavas; Prince Ganapati is taken captive
events.detail: The Kakatiyas' western neighbours, the Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri, were expanding fast. King Mahadeva was killed in a conflict with the Yadava kingdom, dated to 1198-1199, and his son Ganapati was captured. While Ganapati was a prisoner, the Kakatiya kingdom suffered revolts and invasions, and loyal commanders such as Rudra of the Recherla family held it together. The Yadavas eventually released Ganapati and installed him as their vassal, and he married Somaladevi, a daughter of the Yadava king Jaitugi. The kingdom survived, and its greatest reign began under Yadava overlordship.

events.text: c. 1231: Ganapati annexes Velanadu and Divi in the Krishna delta
events.detail: Once free, Ganapati set out to win the rich Telugu-speaking lowlands of coastal Andhra, where the Velanati Choda chiefs had grown weak. His commanders, the Malyala chief Chaunda and his son Kata, campaigned as far as Divi island in the Krishna delta, and by 1201 Kakatiya power reached Vijayawada. Ganapati also backed the Nellore chief Tikka and, according to a 1228 inscription, plundered the Chola capital, probably Kanchi. A 1231 inscription says he annexed Velanadu and Divi. In the 1230s the kingdom reached the Godavari and Krishna deltas, uniting the Telangana uplands with the coast.

events.text: Pandyas kill the Kakatiyas' ally at Muttukuru and take Nellore
events.detail: In the south, Ganapati had long protected the Telugu Choda rulers of Nellore, but a new power was rising: the Pandyas of Madurai under Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan I. While the Kakatiya army was busy fighting the Kadava chief Kopperunchinga, the main Pandya army marched on Nellore. In the Battle of Muttukuru in 1263 the Pandyas captured the city and killed its ruler, Manuma-siddhi II, Ganapati's ally, and also claimed victories over the Kakatiyas and the Seunas. The Kakatiyas lost their southern sphere of influence, a setback that clouded the end of Ganapati's long reign.

events.text: Rudrama Devi becomes sole ruler, one of India's few reigning queens
events.detail: Ganapati had no son, so around 1260 he made his daughter Rudrama co-regent under the male regnal name Rudra-deva Maharaja. By 1263 she appears to have been ruling alone, though she was not formally anointed until at least 1269. She put down an early revolt, recovered some of the lands lost to the Pandyas, and turned back invasions by the Yadavas from the west and the Gajapatis of Odisha from the north-east. She also strengthened Warangal fort, raising its inner wall and adding an outer wall with a moat. The Venetian traveller Marco Polo, who visited around 1293, praised her rule.

events.text: Rudrama Devi dies, probably fighting the rebel chief Ambadeva
events.detail: In the 1270s and 1280s the Kayastha chief Ambadeva, a Kakatiya feudatory, built an independent kingdom in the south of the realm, with support from the Yadavas and the Pandyas. Rudrama lost much of her southern territory to him. An inscription at Chandupatla, dated 27 November 1289, records a gift for the merit of Rudrama and her general Mallikarjuna, who had both recently died, probably in battle against Ambadeva's forces. Older histories had her ruling until 1295. Her grandson Prataparudra II succeeded her and set out to win back the lost lands.

events.text: Kakatiya forces capture Raichur and fortify it
events.detail: Prataparudra II reorganised the army and struck back. In 1291-92 his forces drove Ambadeva out of Tripurantakam, and in 1309 they ended Kayastha rule in Mulikinadu. He also attacked the Yadavas, who had backed Ambadeva. The 1294 Raichur Fort inscription of his feudatory Gona Vithala records the capture of the Adavani and Tumbala forts, in today's Bellary district, and of forts in the Raichur Doab, and says Vithala took Raichur and built strong fortifications there. The Kakatiya kingdom now reached west into the contested lands between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers.

events.text: Kakatiya army repels Delhi's first invasion at Upparapalli
events.detail: Alauddin Khalji, Sultan of Delhi, had already plundered the Yadava capital Devagiri in 1296, and he saw the Kakatiya kingdom as another rich source of plunder. In 1303 he sent an army under Malik Chajju and Fakhruddin Jauna into Telangana. The Kakatiya forces resisted strongly and defeated it at the Battle of Upparapalli, and the expedition ended in disaster. The victory kept the kingdom free for a few more years. But Delhi had shown its interest in the Deccan, and its next attack on Warangal would be far larger and better prepared.

events.text: Malik Kafur besieges Warangal; Prataparudra submits and pays tribute
events.detail: In 1309 Alauddin sent his general Malik Kafur to force Prataparudra to accept Delhi's overlordship. Kafur's army reached Orugallu (Warangal) in January 1310 and breached the outer fort after a siege of about a month. In February Prataparudra surrendered. Alauddin did not want to annex the kingdom: Prataparudra kept his throne but had to make symbolic acts of submission and pay annual tribute. Kafur returned to Delhi in June 1310 with huge wealth, probably including the Koh-i-Noor diamond, along with 20,000 horses and 100 elephants. The kingdom remained, but as a tributary of Delhi.

events.text: Khusrau Khan forces Prataparudra to bow toward Delhi from Warangal's walls
events.detail: After Alauddin died, Prataparudra stopped paying tribute, saying the road to Delhi was too dangerous. In 1318 the new sultan, Mubarak Shah, sent his general Khusrau Khan to Orugallu with siege machines never before seen in the region. Prataparudra had to submit again. This time Delhi arranged a very public humiliation: the king bowed towards Delhi from the ramparts of his own capital. His annual tribute was reset at 100 elephants and 12,000 horses, and he had to give up five districts. The kingdom still kept its own king, but its independence was now a fiction.

events.text: Prataparudra breaks with Delhi; the first Tughluq siege of Warangal fails
events.detail: In 1320 a revolution in Delhi replaced the Khaljis with Ghiyasuddin Tughluq, and Prataparudra asserted his independence again. In 1321 the new sultan sent his son, Jauna Khan, to besiege Orugallu. The siege dragged on for about six months. Rumours of the sultan's death split Jauna Khan's army, many officers left, and the attackers withdrew to Devagiri to regroup. Prataparudra celebrated by opening his grain stores for public feasting. The victory seemed to restore the kingdom, but it left Warangal short of supplies when the enemy came back.

events.text: Jauna Khan takes Warangal; the Kakatiya kingdom is annexed by Delhi
events.detail: Jauna Khan, the future Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq, returned in 1323 with a reinforced army. After a five-month siege, with few supplies left, Prataparudra was forced to submit, and the Kakatiya dynasty article dates the end of the dynasty to 9 November 1323. Orugallu was renamed Sultanpur and the kingdom became a province of the Delhi Sultanate. Prataparudra died while being taken to Delhi as a prisoner, perhaps by suicide on the banks of the Narmada. Telugu chiefs such as Kapaya Nayaka later held Warangal, but the Kakatiya line was over.

name: Seuna (Yadava) dynasty of Devagiri
summary: The Seunas, or Yadavas of Devagiri, were Chalukya feudatories until Bhillama V seized Kalyani around 1187, declared himself king and built the hill fortress of Devagiri. Under Simhana II (c. 1200/1210–1246) they ruled the western Deccan from the Narmada to the Tungabhadra, and Marathi became a language of government and literature under their rule. Alauddin Khalji's raid of 1296 made them tributaries of Delhi, Malik Kafur took Devagiri in 1307–08 and again in 1313, and the kingdom was annexed in 1317.

events.text: c. 1190: Hoysala king Ballala II routs Bhillama V at Soratur
events.detail: Bhillama V became Yadava ruler around 1175, while his nominal overlords, the Chalukyas of Kalyani, were collapsing. Around 1187 he took the old Chalukya capital, Kalyani, declared himself a sovereign king and founded a new capital at Devagiri, a formidable natural hill stronghold. But the Hoysala king Veera Ballala II was also claiming the Chalukya lands. In the late 1180s, or around 1191 by another account, Ballala decisively defeated Bhillama's army at Soratur, in present-day Gadag district. The Yadavas were driven north of the Malaprabha and Krishna rivers, which formed their southern border for the next two decades.

events.text: c. 1194: Jaitugi invades the Kakatiya kingdom and forces its submission
events.detail: Bhillama's son Jaitugi, king from about 1191, turned east against the Kakatiyas of Telangana. The Seuna dynasty article dates his invasion to around 1194. The Kakatiya king Mahadeva was killed in the fighting around 1198-1199, and some historians think his predecessor Rudradeva had also died fighting Jaitugi. Mahadeva's son Ganapati was taken captive and later released as a Yadava vassal, marrying Jaitugi's daughter. For years the Kakatiyas accepted Yadava overlordship, giving Devagiri influence over much of the eastern Deccan as well as the west.

events.text: c. 1213: Simhana II annexes Hoysala lands up to the Tungabhadra
events.detail: Jaitugi's son Simhana II, who came to the throne around 1200 or 1210, is regarded as the dynasty's greatest king. While the Hoysalas were busy in the Tamil south, he pushed across the Malaprabha. Yadava inscriptions appear there from 1202, and by 1213 most of present-day Dharwad district had been annexed. Banavasi fell before 1215, and by 1220 everything north of the Tungabhadra was his. The Rattas of Saundatti, former Hoysala vassals, became his feudatories and helped him expand south. The Yadava kingdom's southern frontier now ran along the Tungabhadra river.

events.text: Simhana invades the Paramara kingdom of Malwa
events.detail: To the north, across the Narmada, lay Malwa, ruled by the Paramara dynasty. In 1215 Simhana invaded it successfully. His court poet Hemadri later claimed that the Paramara king Arjunavarman was killed, but an inscription of 1222 mentions only his defeat, so the claim is doubtful. The raid brought plunder and prestige rather than new land. Malwa stayed Paramara, and the Narmada remained roughly the northern limit of Yadava power. Later Yadava kings defeated the weakening Paramaras again before 1250 and in the 1270s, without annexing their land.

events.text: c. 1216: Simhana annexes the Shilahara kingdom of Kolhapur
events.detail: The Shilaharas of Kolhapur, in the south-west of present-day Maharashtra, had been feudatories but had asserted their independence under King Bhoja II. In 1216 Simhana attacked him, and Bhoja fled to the hill fort of Panhala. The Shilahara territory, including Kolhapur, appears to have been annexed before 1217. Simhana's general Bichana later subdued other restless southern chiefs, among them the Guttas of Dharwad and the Kadambas of Hangal and Goa. At its height Simhana's kingdom probably stretched from the Narmada to the Tungabhadra and from the Arabian Sea to western Telangana.

events.text: Simhana's general Kholeshvara conquers Lata in southern Gujarat
events.detail: Lata, a coastal region of present-day Gujarat, kept shifting its loyalty between the Yadavas, the Paramaras and the Chaulukyas of Gujarat. In 1220 Simhana sent his general Kholeshvara there. Kholeshvara killed the local ruler Simha and captured Lata, and Simhana made Simha's relative Shankha a Yadava vassal. The Chaulukya general Lavanaprasada struck back and took the port of Khambhat, and Shankha's counter-attacks with Yadava help failed. The struggle ended in a peace treaty around 1232. A later Yadava invasion of Gujarat in the 1240s failed, and the general Rama, Kholeshvara's son, was killed.

events.text: c. 1263: Mahadeva invades the Kakatiya kingdom but is driven back
events.detail: Simhana's grandson Krishna (c. 1246-1261) fought inconclusive wars with the Paramaras, the Vaghelas of Gujarat and the Hoysalas. His younger brother Mahadeva (c. 1261-1270) saw an opening in the east, where the new Kakatiya queen Rudrama Devi faced rebellions. He invaded Telangana, and Yadava records boast of victories over the ruler of Tilinga. But a Kakatiya inscription says their general Bhairava defeated the Yadava army, probably in or after 1263, and the invasion appears to have been repulsed. Mahadeva's invasion of the Hoysala kingdom was also turned back. The age of easy Yadava expansion was over.

events.text: c. 1271: Ramachandra seizes the throne and raids his neighbours
events.detail: When Mahadeva died around 1270 his son Ammana became king, but after a short reign he was dethroned by his cousin Ramachandra, son of King Krishna. Ramachandra pursued an aggressive policy. In the 1270s he defeated the weakened Paramaras of Malwa, and in 1275 his general Tikkama led a powerful army into the Hoysala kingdom, gathering great plunder before he was forced to retreat in 1276. Ramachandra also pushed the north-eastern frontier, subduing Bhandara and occupying Tripuri, the old Kalachuri capital near Jabalpur. But he lost Raichur and other lands to the Kakatiyas.

events.text: c. 1290: Dnyaneshwar writes the Dnyaneshwari in Marathi
events.detail: The Yadavas were the first major dynasty to use Marathi as an official language, and early Marathi literature emerged under their rule. Hemadri, a minister at the Yadava court, tried to formalise Marathi with Sanskrit expressions to raise its status. Around 1290, during Ramachandra's reign, the saint-poet Dnyaneshwar wrote the Dnyaneshwari, a Marathi commentary on the Bhagavad Gita, bringing a sacred Sanskrit text into the everyday language. The Mahanubhava sect also spread Marathi as a literary language. The Yadava age left a lasting cultural mark on the region even as its political power waned.

events.text: Alauddin Khalji raids Devagiri; Ramachandra agrees to pay tribute
events.detail: In 1296 Alauddin Khalji, then governor of Kara for the Delhi Sultanate, led a secret raid across the Vindhyas, spreading word that he was heading for Chanderi. He reached Devagiri while the main Yadava army was away under Ramachandra's son Simhana and the fort was short of supplies. Ramachandra withdrew into the hilltop citadel while the lower city was plundered. When Simhana returned and fought, he was defeated, and the Yadavas agreed to a much larger indemnity and tribute from the Achalpur province. Alauddin used the wealth to seize the Delhi throne, but the tribute went unpaid.

events.text: c. 1307: Malik Kafur takes Devagiri; Ramachandra becomes Delhi's vassal
events.detail: Ramachandra's unpaid tribute kept mounting. In 1307 (some sources say 1308) Alauddin, now sultan, sent his general Malik Kafur with a huge army, helped by the governors of Malwa and Gujarat. They overcame Devagiri's weakened forces almost without a battle, and Ramachandra was taken to Delhi. Alauddin reinstated him as a tributary ruler in return for help against the kingdoms farther south. Devagiri became Delhi's base in the Deccan: in 1310 Kafur marched from there against the Kakatiyas, and in 1311 against the Hoysalas. The Yadava kingdom survived only as a client of Delhi.

events.text: Simhana III defies Delhi and is killed; Kafur occupies Devagiri
events.detail: Ramachandra died around 1311, and his successor Simhana III, also called Shankaradeva, challenged Delhi's supremacy and refused to keep paying tribute. In 1313 Alauddin sent Malik Kafur back to Devagiri. Simhana III was killed in the fighting, and the Khalji army occupied the city. Kafur stayed on as governor for about two years, turning the Yadava capital into a Delhi province in all but name. A last king, Harapaladeva, held the Yadava title from 1313, but real power in the western Deccan had passed to the sultans of Delhi.

events.text: The last Yadava king falls; Delhi annexes the kingdom
events.detail: After Alauddin Khalji died and Mubarak Shah took over in Delhi in 1316, the Yadava prince Harapaladeva ruled briefly as the dynasty's last king. In 1317, according to the Seuna dynasty article, the kingdom was annexed outright by the Khalji sultanate, ending some 130 years of Yadava sovereignty (the same article elsewhere gives 1308, when Ramachandra became a vassal). Devagiri became the seat of Delhi's power in the Deccan, and Muhammad bin Tughluq later renamed it Daulatabad. Thirty years later, rebel Delhi officers at Daulatabad founded the Bahmani Sultanate.
