name: Vijayanagara Empire
summary: Founded in 1336 by the brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty, Vijayanagara absorbed the last Hoysala lands by 1346 and the Madurai Sultanate by 1378, uniting the Hindu kingdoms of the south. For two centuries it fought the Bahmani sultans and their successors for the Raichur Doab, and under Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529) it covered almost all of India south of the Krishna river. In 1565 the allied Deccan sultanates crushed its army at Talikota and sacked the capital; the Aravidu kings ruled on from Penukonda and later Chandragiri and Vellore until 1646.

events.text: c. 1346: Harihara I takes over the last Hoysala lands
events.detail: Vijayanagara was born in the chaos left by Delhi's invasions of the south. In 1336 the brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family, commanders who had served the Hoysala king, founded a new state on the Tungabhadra river; later tradition credits the sage Vidyaranya of Sringeri with inspiring them. After the Hoysala king Veera Ballala III was killed fighting the Sultan of Madurai in 1343, his kingdom crumbled, and by 1346 its lands had merged into the Vijayanagara realm. That year Harihara I and the Hoysala queen made grants to the Sringeri monastery on the same day.

events.text: Bahmani guns defeat Vijayanagara at Adoni in the first great war
events.detail: To the north lay the Bahmani Sultanate, founded in 1347 by rebel Delhi officers in the Deccan. The two states fought over the fertile Tungabhadra-Krishna doab, the Godavari basin and the Marathwada country. The wars with Sultan Mohammed Shah I were savage: the historian Firishta wrote that the population of the Carnatic took generations to recover. At the Battle of Adoni in 1368 the Bahmanis used a train of artillery, often called the first recorded use of firearms in South Asia, though historians debate this. The doab between the rivers would be fought over for two centuries.

events.text: Madurai Sultanate destroyed; Vijayanagara rules the far south
events.detail: In 1335 the Delhi governor of Madurai had founded an independent Madurai Sultanate, which killed the Hoysala king in 1343. Bukka Raya I's son Kumara Kampana led Vijayanagara's armies south, first destroying the Sambuvaraya dynasty and then invading the sultanate; the historian Bowman dates the conquest to about 1370, and the Srirangam temple was restored in 1371. The last sultan, Ala-ud-Din Sikandar Shah, was killed at Madurai in 1378, and Vijayanagara took formal possession under Harihara II. Kampana's wife Gangadevi celebrated the war in a Sanskrit poem, the Madhura Vijayam. Vijayanagara now reached the southern tip of India.

events.text: Deva Raya I loses to Firuz Shah, pays tribute and gives him a daughter
events.detail: The wars over the doab went on under Harihara II (1377-1404), who consolidated the empire beyond the Krishna, and under his son Deva Raya I. The Bahmani sultan Firuz Shah defeated Vijayanagara in 1398 and again in 1406. The peace that followed, dated 1407 in the Vijayanagara article, required Deva Raya to pay an annual tribute of 100,000 huns, five maunds of pearls and fifty elephants, and to give his daughter to the sultan in marriage. When Vijayanagara stopped paying, the Bahmanis invaded again in 1417. Such tribute wars recurred throughout the 15th century.

events.text: Vijayanagara routs Firuz Shah at Pangal and wins back the eastern districts
events.detail: The tide turned in 1420. Firuz Shah attacked the fort of Pangal, but the campaign went badly for him: his army was beaten, and he retreated and gave up the southern and eastern districts of his kingdom. The defeat broke him, and in 1422 he was forced to abdicate in favour of his brother Ahmad Shah. For Vijayanagara, Pangal undid the humiliation of 1406 and strengthened its hold on the eastern doab. Deva Raya I died in 1422; after the brief reigns of Ramachandra Raya and Vira Vijaya Bukka Raya, Deva Raya II came to the throne.

events.text: Deva Raya II begins the golden age of the Sangama dynasty
events.detail: Deva Raya II, king from 1424, is considered by many the greatest ruler of the Sangama dynasty. He quelled rebellious lords and the Zamorin of Calicut and the ruler of Quilon in Kerala, and his commander Lakkanna collected tribute in Sri Lanka. By 1436 the chiefs of Kondavidu and the Velama rulers had accepted his overlordship, and he fought the Gajapatis of Odisha several times. He wrote in Kannada and Sanskrit and patronised poets such as Kumara Vyasa and Srinatha. The Persian envoy Abdur Razzak, writing around 1443, said the empire stretched from Ceylon to Gulbarga.

events.text: War with the Bahmanis; Vijayanagara falls back to Mudgal
events.detail: After some years of peace, war with the Bahmani Sultanate broke out again in 1443. Firishta blamed Deva Raya II's military build-up, which included recruiting many Muslim archers and cavalry; Abdur Razzak said the sultan exploited a revolt at Vijayanagara, including a brother's attempt to assassinate the king, who was wounded. The fighting brought some successes and some reversals. In the end Vijayanagara forces fell back to Mudgal, and some land between the Tungabhadra and Krishna was lost. The Bahmani sultan later celebrated with the Chand Minar at Daulatabad. It was the last major conflict between the two powers.

events.text: Deva Raya II dies; the Gajapatis of Odisha seize the eastern lands
events.detail: Deva Raya II died in 1446 and was succeeded by his son Mallikarjuna Raya. The Gajapati king of Odisha took advantage, occupying the Reddi kingdoms of Rajahmundry and Kondaveedu and reaching Kanchipuram and Tiruchirappalli, ending Vijayanagara control over much of the Tamil country. An inscription mocked the Gajapati as 'a yawning lion to the sheep of the Karnatak King'. Under Mallikarjuna's successor Virupaksha Raya II, Goa and much of Karnataka were lost to the Bahmani Sultanate. The empire was shrinking on several sides at once, and its prestige had fallen far.

events.text: Saluva Narasimha seizes the throne and wins back lost provinces
events.detail: Virupaksha Raya II's governor Saluva Narasimha limited the damage. He held almost all of coastal Andhra south of the Krishna, Chittoor, the two Arcots and Kolar, defeated the Gajapatis and took Udayagiri, drove the Pandyas from Tanjore and recovered most of the empire's earlier losses. After Virupaksha Raya II died in 1485, Saluva Narasimha led a coup that ended the Sangama dynasty and founded the Saluva dynasty. He left his young sons in the care of the general Tuluva Narasa Nayaka, who ruled as regent until 1503 and defended the empire against the Gajapatis and the Bahmanis.

events.text: Krishnadevaraya takes the throne and defeats the Deccan sultans at Diwani
events.detail: In 1503 Narasa Nayaka's son Vira Narasimha had the last Saluva prince killed and began the Tuluva dynasty, but nobles revolted and neighbours encroached. In 1509 his brother Krishnadevaraya came to the throne. That year his forces clashed with the Bahmani sultan Mahmud and Bijapur's Yusuf Adil Shah at Diwani; Mahmud was wounded and defeated, Yusuf was killed, and the Raichur Doab was annexed, according to his biography. Krishnadevaraya then released Mahmud and restored him as ruler. In 1510 he made friends with the Portuguese in Goa, buying guns and Arabian horses from them.

events.text: c. 1513: Krishnadevaraya takes Udayagiri from the Gajapatis
events.detail: Krishnadevaraya then turned east against the resurgent Gajapati kingdom of Odisha under King Prataparudra, which held the coastal Andhra forts. The siege of Udayagiri began in 1512 and lasted about a year. Next Kondaveedu fell to a night attack led by his minister Timmarusu. Prataparudra eventually came to terms, giving his daughter Jaganmohini to Krishnadevaraya in marriage, and the Krishna river became the boundary between the two kingdoms. A defeat at Pangal by Sultan Quli Qutb Shah of Golconda in 1513 showed the limits of his power, but the east coast south of the Krishna was now Vijayanagara's.

events.text: Krishnadevaraya captures Raichur from Bijapur
events.detail: Raichur, the great fortress of the doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra, had changed hands many times. In 1520 Krishnadevaraya besieged it, held by Ismail Adil Shah of Bijapur, with an army said to number hundreds of thousands of foot soldiers. On 19 May 1520, after a hard siege in which some 16,000 Vijayanagara soldiers are said to have died, the fortress fell, with help from Portuguese gunners under Cristovao de Figueiredo. Krishnadevaraya went on to occupy Bijapur and later razed Gulbarga. The empire was at its peak, and Babur considered him the most powerful ruler in India.

events.text: Civil war ends; Rama Raya becomes the real ruler under Sadasiva Raya
events.detail: Krishnadevaraya was followed by his half-brother Achyuta Deva Raya (1529-1542). When Achyuta died in June 1542, his brother-in-law Salakaraju Tirumala took power as regent for the boy king Venkata I, had him killed and even invited the Sultan of Bijapur to help him. Outraged nobles rallied to Rama Raya, Krishnadevaraya's son-in-law, who backed Achyuta's nephew Sadasiva Raya. In 1543 Salakaraju was defeated and killed at the Battle of the Tungabhadra. Sadasiva became emperor, but Rama Raya held real power for the next two decades, meddling in the quarrels of the Deccan sultanates.

events.text: The Deccan sultanates crush Vijayanagara at Talikota; the capital is sacked
events.detail: Rama Raya's policy of playing the sultanates off against one another finally united them against him. Ahmadnagar, Bijapur, Golconda and Bidar joined forces, and on 23 January 1565 they met his army near Talikota, by the Krishna river. The battle seemed to be going Vijayanagara's way until, according to some accounts, two Muslim generals in its service, the Gilani brothers, changed sides. Rama Raya was captured and beheaded, and his army fled in confusion. The sultanate armies plundered the capital unopposed; its royal centre was never rebuilt, and the empire's centre of gravity moved south.

events.text: c. 1567: Tirumala moves the court to Penukonda; Aravidu kings rule on
events.detail: Tirumala Deva Raya, one of the Vijayanagara commanders at Talikota, escaped with the army. He tried to regroup at Vijayanagara and used the ruined city for about two years, then founded a new capital at Penukonda and began the Aravidu dynasty. In 1572 he abdicated, dividing what remained among his three sons. The Aravidu kings later moved their capital to Chandragiri (1592) and Vellore (1604), but central authority collapsed in 1614 and the empire ended in 1646. Nayaka rulers at Madurai, Tanjore, Gingee, Mysore and Keladi became independent kingdoms.

name: Bahmani Sultanate
summary: The Bahmani Sultanate was born on 3 August 1347, when rebel officers of the Delhi Sultanate in the Deccan crowned Zafar Khan (Hasan Gangu) as Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah, with his capital at Gulbarga. The first independent Muslim sultanate of the Deccan, it fought Vijayanagara and Warangal for over a century, moved its capital to Bidar around 1429 and reached its greatest extent under the minister Mahmud Gawan. Factional strife and Gawan's execution in 1481 broke it apart: its governors declared independence from 1490, and it dissolved into the five Deccan Sultanates by 1527.

events.text: Kapaya Nayaka of Warangal gives the sultan the Turquoise Throne
events.detail: Ala-ud-Din Bahman Shah died in 1358 and was succeeded by his son Mohammed Shah I, who spent much of his reign suppressing banditry and fighting his Hindu neighbours, Vijayanagara and, at times, Warangal. Warangal was then ruled by Kapaya Nayaka, a Telugu king of the post-Kakatiya era. He reportedly gave the sultan a jewelled throne, the Takht-e-Firoza or Turquoise Throne. According to the historian Firishta, it replaced Bahman Shah's silver throne on 23 March 1363. The gift marked Bahmani superiority over Warangal, the eastern rival the sultanate would finally conquer some sixty years later.

events.text: Mohammed Shah I builds the great Jama Masjid of Gulbarga
events.detail: Gulbarga, which the founder called Hasanabad, was the Bahmani capital, where all his coins were minted. In 1367 Mohammed Shah I built its Jama Masjid with the help of a Persian architect, Rafi of Qazvin. The mosque reflected the Persianate culture of the Bahmani court, where Persian was the official language and the Persian new year, Nowruz, was celebrated; Mohammed Shah had even ascended the throne on Nowruz. Soldiers, scholars and saints moved from Delhi and northern India to the new Deccan capital, which became the heart of a distinctive Indo-Persian culture in the south.

events.text: Bahmani artillery defeats Vijayanagara at the Battle of Adoni
events.detail: Mohammed Shah I fought savage wars with Vijayanagara over the Tungabhadra-Krishna doab, the Godavari basin and the Marathwada country. The historian Firishta wrote that the population of the Carnatic took generations to recover. At the Battle of Adoni in 1368 the Bahmani army used a train of artillery against Vijayanagara. This is often called the first recorded use of firearms in South Asia, though the historian Iqtidar Alam Khan argues that the Bahmanis got the weapons from Delhi and that others already had them. Either way, gunpowder weapons became the backbone of the Bahmani army.

events.text: Firuz Shah seizes the throne after a palace coup
events.detail: After the peaceful reign of Muhammad Shah II (1378-1397), the dynasty fell into turmoil. In 1397 his young son Ghiyasuddin was blinded and imprisoned by the Turkic slave Taghalchin, who put a puppet, Shamsuddin, on the throne. Firuz and Ahmad, grandsons of the founder, marched on Gulbarga, defeated and killed Taghalchin, and in November 1397 Firuz became sultan. He brought Hindus into high office, welcomed Sufis such as Gesudaraz to his court, and was the first author to write in Dakhni, the Deccan form of Urdu. He also founded the city of Firozabad near Gulbarga.

events.text: Firuz defeats Vijayanagara and marries Deva Raya I's daughter
events.detail: Firuz Shah fought Vijayanagara on many occasions. Early in his reign he turned back Harihara II's advance into the Raichur Doab, and he won victories in 1398 and 1406. The 1406 war ended in a treaty under which Deva Raya I gave his daughter to the sultan in marriage and, according to the Vijayanagara article, agreed to pay a heavy annual tribute of 100,000 huns, pearls and fifty elephants. The Raichur Doab stayed in Bahmani hands for the moment. When Vijayanagara stopped paying, war broke out again, and in 1417 it went against the Bahmanis.

events.text: Firuz Shah is defeated at Pangal and loses his southern and eastern districts
events.detail: In 1420 Firuz Shah attacked the fort of Pangal, but the campaign ended in disaster. He retreated and gave up the southern and eastern districts of his kingdom, a serious loss of territory, and he was a broken man afterwards. To secure the throne for his son Hasan Khan, he ordered his capable brother Ahmad blinded. Ahmad rebelled and besieged Gulbarga, and in 1422 Firuz abdicated in his favour, dying soon after. He was buried in the Haft Gumbaz tombs at Gulbarga, and his brother began a far more aggressive reign.

events.text: c. 1425: Ahmad Shah I conquers what remains of Warangal
events.detail: Ahmad Shah I, sultan from 1422, spent his reign at war. He fought Vijayanagara in 1423 and campaigned against Warangal in 1424-1425, finally capturing the remnants of the Warangal kingdom in eastern Telangana. He annexed Mahur in the north by 1427, after three campaigns, and fought the sultans of Malwa and Gujarat from 1425 to 1435. Chroniclers also describe his massacres, including the killing of the Raja of Mahur after his surrender. The conquest of Warangal pushed the Bahmani frontier east across Telangana, into the old heartland of the Kakatiya kings.

events.text: c. 1429: The capital moves from Gulbarga to Bidar
events.detail: Ahmad Shah I moved the Bahmani capital north-east from Gulbarga to Bidar, where he built the great Bidar Fort. The Bahmani Sultanate article dates the move to 1429, the article on Ahmad Shah to 1432, and the Deva Raya II article to around 1426. After settling in Bidar, Ahmad Shah converted to Shi'ism, and he and his successors began to recruit foreigners from overseas into their service. This planted the rivalry between the newcomers, the Afaqis, and the older Deccani nobility, descendants of the first settlers from northern India, that would later tear the sultanate apart.

events.text: Ala-ud-Din Ahmad II defeats Vijayanagara's Deva Raya II
events.detail: Ahmad Shah's son Ala-ud-Din Ahmad II, sultan from 1436, faced a revived Vijayanagara under Deva Raya II, who had built up his army with Muslim archers and cavalry. War broke out in 1443. After mixed fortunes, Vijayanagara forces fell back to Mudgal and lost some land between the Tungabhadra and Krishna. In 1445 the sultan was honoured with the Chand Minar, a tall minaret at Daulatabad, for the victory, which was the last major conflict between the two powers. At home, though, rivalry between Deccani and foreign nobles grew, and in 1446 a massacre of Persian Shi'a nobles shook the court.

events.text: Mahmud Gawan becomes prime minister and real ruler of the sultanate
events.detail: Mahmud Gawan was a Persian merchant who landed at the port of Dabhol in 1453, aged 42, intending to sell horses to the Bahmani court. Sultan Ala-ud-Din Ahmad II received him well, and Humayun Shah made him chief minister. Under the boy sultans Nizam Shah and Muhammad Shah III he served as regent, and from 1466 he was prime minister and the real ruler of the state. He helped push back a Gajapati invasion from Odisha that came near Bidar, repelled several attacks from Malwa, and in 1469 won the Konkan from Vijayanagara. Under him the sultanate reached its greatest extent.

events.text: Gawan captures Goa and Dabhol on the west coast
events.detail: Gawan, who had first come to the Deccan to sell horses, understood the value of the west coast ports. In February 1472 he captured Goa, long held by Vijayanagara, along with Dabhol, and he took Belgaum using mines and explosives; Bahmani cannon had already been used in the siege of Machal fort in 1470 or 1471. The conquests gave the sultanate a coastline on the Arabian Sea and its widest territory. In the same year Gawan completed his madrasa at Bidar, a great college of religious and secular learning with a library of about 3,000 manuscripts.

events.text: Gawan doubles the provinces to eight and curbs the governors
events.detail: To hold such a large state together, Mahmud Gawan reformed its government in 1473. He increased the provinces (tarafs) from four to eight, dividing them equally between Deccani and foreign nobles, limited each provincial governor to a single fort, and standardised the nobles' obligations to the crown. The reforms strengthened the sultan's grip, but many nobles resented losing power. Gawan, a foreign-born Persian, was also caught between the two great factions: the Dakhanis, the Deccan's Sunni elite descended from northern settlers, and the Afaqis, mostly Shi'a newcomers from the west.

events.text: Mahmud Gawan is executed over a forged letter
events.detail: Gawan's enemies, angered by reforms that curbed their power, forged a letter that seemed to show him inviting the Gajapati king Purushottama Deva of Odisha to invade. Sultan Muhammad Shah III believed it and on 5 April 1481 had his minister executed, an act he regretted until his own death in 1482. The plot's chief architect, Malik Hasan, also known as Nizam-ul-Mulk Bahri, succeeded Gawan as prime minister and became regent for the next sultan, Mahmud Shah. Without Gawan the sultanate fell into disarray, and power drained from the throne to the provincial governors.

events.text: Governors of Ahmadnagar, Bijapur and Berar declare their independence
events.detail: Mahmud Shah, sultan from 1482, was the last Bahmani ruler with real power, and even he depended on his ministers. In 1490 three provincial governors, Malik Ahmad Nizam Shah I of Ahmadnagar, Yusuf Adil Shah of Bijapur and Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk of Berar, agreed to assert their independence and founded their own sultanates, though they still professed loyalty to the sultan. Golconda and Bidar soon became independent in practice too. The last Bahmani sultans were puppets of their Barid Shahi ministers, and after 1518 the state broke up into the five Deccan Sultanates; it was formally dissolved in 1527.

name: Sikh Empire
summary: As Mughal power collapsed in the 18th century, Sikh bands organised into misls fought the Afghan armies of Ahmad Shah Durrani and divided the Punjab among a confederacy of chiefs. Ranjit Singh of the Sukerchakia misl took Lahore in 1799, was crowned Maharaja in 1801 and united the Punjab, then conquered Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar. After his death in 1839, court murders and an overmighty army weakened the state; two wars with the British East India Company followed, and the Punjab was annexed in 1849.

events.text: Vadda Ghallughara: Ahmad Shah Durrani's army massacres Sikhs at Kup
events.detail: In 1748 the Sikh fighting bands of the Punjab were reorganised into misls under one army, the Dal Khalsa, commanded by Jassa Singh Ahluwalia. They fought the Mughal governors and the Afghan ruler Ahmad Shah Durrani, who invaded India repeatedly. In 1762 Durrani's army caught a large Sikh force at Kup and killed thousands of people, a disaster remembered as the Vadda Ghallughara, the 'great massacre'. Yet the Sikhs recovered remarkably fast: about six months later they defeated the Afghans at Amritsar, and Durrani could not crush them.

events.text: The misls capture Sirhind and share out the land from Karnal to Ferozepur
events.detail: Sirhind, between the Sutlej and the Yamuna, was held for Ahmad Shah Durrani as the key to the eastern Punjab. In 1764 the misls captured it, and the territory between Karnal and Ferozepur was divided among several misls and administered jointly. The Phulkian misl held much of this southern Malwa region, between Sirhind and Delhi, and its states later survived as the Cis-Sutlej states, outside Ranjit Singh's kingdom. The capture carried Sikh power towards Delhi and showed that Durrani could no longer hold the eastern Punjab.

events.text: Three Sikh chiefs take Lahore and rule the city as a triumvirate
events.detail: Lahore, the old capital of the Punjab, changed hands several times during the Afghan wars; the Sikhs won a siege of the city in 1761 and began striking their own coins. From 1765 Lahore was ruled by a triumvirate of Sikh chiefs, and the Bhangi misl, the strongest power in the Majha region, came to dominate western Punjab, including Lahore and Amritsar. By the 1770s more than sixty Sikh-ruled principalities lay between the Yamuna and the Indus, many funded by the rakhi system of protection payments. The confederacy was powerful but divided.

events.text: Ranjit Singh of the Sukerchakia misl captures Lahore (7 July)
events.detail: Ranjit Singh, born in 1780, became chief of the Sukerchakia misl at the age of twelve when his father Maha Singh died in 1792. The Afghan ruler Zaman Shah Durrani invaded the Punjab in 1797–98 but soon retreated. On 7 July 1799 Ranjit Singh captured Lahore from the triumvirate that had held it since 1765, and Zaman Shah later recognised his hold on the city. Ranjit Singh moved his capital there from Gujranwala, founded by his grandfather Charat Singh. The capture made the Sukerchakias the leading misl and is counted as the beginning of the Sikh Empire.

events.text: Ranjit Singh is crowned Maharaja of the Punjab at Lahore (12 April)
events.detail: On 12 April 1801 Ranjit Singh was formally crowned at Lahore by Sahib Singh Bedi, a descendant of Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith. The ceremony turned a misl chief into a sovereign Maharaja and marks the formal beginning of the Sikh Empire. He had already annexed the Jammu region in 1800. Over the following decade he absorbed the other misls one by one, building a single kingdom in the Punjab where there had been dozens of rival chiefs. Only the Phulkian and other chiefs south of the Sutlej stayed outside his rule.

events.text: Ranjit Singh takes Amritsar, the Sikh holy city, from the Bhangi misl
events.detail: Amritsar, home of the Harmandir Sahib (the Golden Temple), was the spiritual centre of the Sikhs, and the Bhangi misl held it. In 1802, aged 22, Ranjit Singh took Amritsar from the Bhangis. Winning the holy city gave him great prestige among Sikhs. It also began his conquest of the remaining misls, which was largely complete by 1812: Kasur and Jhang were annexed in 1807, and by 1813 all the remaining misls had been absorbed. The Sikh Empire now covered the central Punjab, from the Sutlej towards the Indus.

events.text: Treaty of Amritsar with the British fixes the Sutlej as the eastern border
events.detail: As Ranjit Singh's power grew he looked across the Sutlej, where the Phulkian and other Sikh chiefs ruled and where his forces occupied Faridkot in 1807. There his ambitions ran into those of the British East India Company. In 1809 the two sides signed the Treaty of Amritsar, which set the Sutlej as the eastern boundary of Ranjit Singh's kingdom; he returned Faridkot to its ruler. The treaty kept peace with the British for more than thirty years and turned Ranjit Singh's expansion north and west, against the Afghans.

events.text: Mohkam Chand defeats the Afghans at Attock and seizes the Indus fort
events.detail: Attock, a fort guarding the crossing of the Indus, was held by the Afghan Durrani kingdom. In 1813 Ranjit Singh's general Mohkam Chand defeated the Afghan army in the Battle of Attock and captured the fort. It gave the Sikhs a strong point on the Indus and a gateway towards Peshawar and the north-west. The same year the last independent misls were annexed, so the Sikh kingdom now stretched across the Punjab from the Sutlej to the Indus, and the stage was set for war with the Afghans over Multan and Kashmir.

events.text: Multan falls to the Sikhs, ending Afghan rule in the southern Punjab
events.detail: Multan, an ancient walled city in the southern Punjab, had been held by the Bhangi misl until the Afghan Durranis took it back in 1780. Since then it had been ruled by Afghan governors. In 1818 Ranjit Singh's son Kharak Singh and the general Misr Diwan Chand captured the city, ending Afghan influence east of the Indus. Multan gave the empire a large new province reaching towards the borders of Sindh, and its fall freed the Sikh army for a campaign against Kashmir the following year.

events.text: Victory at Shopian brings the Kashmir Valley into the empire
events.detail: The Kashmir Valley was still ruled by governors of the Afghan Durrani kingdom. In 1819 a Sikh army defeated the Afghans at the Battle of Shopian, and Kashmir was annexed to the Sikh Empire. The same year the Namgyal kings of Ladakh, further east, began paying annual tribute to Lahore. In 1820 Ranjit Singh confirmed the Dogra Gulab Singh in his family's estates at Jammu, and the Dogras became powerful vassals in the hills. Kashmir remained one of the empire's most valuable provinces until it was lost in 1846.

events.text: Peshawar is annexed; the Dogra general Zorawar Singh conquers Ladakh
events.detail: Ranjit Singh pushed west into Pashtun country. After the Battle of Nowshera in 1823, Peshawar paid tribute to Lahore, and in 1834 the Sikhs took the city from the Peshawar Sardars and formally annexed it. In the same year Zorawar Singh, general of Ranjit Singh's Dogra vassal Gulab Singh, conquered the Namgyal kingdom of Ladakh, and Baltistan was brought under Sikh suzerainty in 1839–40. The empire now reached from the Khyber Pass in the west to Ladakh in the Himalaya, and from the Sutlej to the borders of Sindh.

events.text: Hari Singh Nalwa is killed holding Jamrud against an Afghan army
events.detail: The Afghan emir Dost Mohammad Khan never accepted the loss of Peshawar. While many of the best Sikh troops were at a royal wedding in Lahore, he sent his son Wazir Akbar Khan with a large army against the Sikh fort at Jamrud, at the mouth of the Khyber Pass. In the battle on 30 April 1837 the Sikh commander Hari Singh Nalwa was mortally wounded, but the garrison held out until reinforcements arrived. Historians disagree over who won, but the Afghans withdrew, Peshawar stayed Sikh, and Jamrud was the last battle with the Afghans on the western frontier.

events.text: Ranjit Singh dies (27 June); succession struggles shake the Lahore court
events.detail: Ranjit Singh died in his sleep at Lahore on 27 June 1839. He left a large, well-trained army, built with the help of European officers such as Jean-François Allard and Jean-Baptiste Ventura, but no strong successor. His son Kharak Singh, his grandson Nau Nihal Singh, the regent Chand Kaur and Sher Singh followed one another within a few years, each killed or removed amid court intrigue. In 1843 the child Duleep Singh became Maharaja with his mother Jind Kaur as regent, while the army, which grew to over 80,000 men by 1845, became ever more powerful.

events.text: Defeat at Sobraon; the Treaty of Lahore takes the Jullundur Doab and Kashmir
events.detail: Tension with the British grew as both sides massed troops on the Sutlej. On 11 December 1845 the Sikh army crossed the river, and the British declared war. Led by the vizier Lal Singh and the commander Tej Singh, whom Sikh historians accuse of treachery, the Sikhs lost at Mudki, Ferozeshah and Aliwal. On 10 February 1846, at Sobraon, their bridge broke and thousands died. The Treaty of Lahore (9 March 1846) took the Jullundur Doab and, in place of an indemnity, Kashmir and Hazara; the British sold Kashmir to Gulab Singh. By December a British resident effectively governed the rest of the kingdom.

events.text: Revolt at Multan begins the Second Anglo-Sikh War
events.detail: In April 1848 two British officials, Vans Agnew and Anderson, were attacked at Multan and murdered on 19 April. The governor, Diwan Mulraj, was pulled into open rebellion, and the rising spread: Chattar Singh Attariwala rebelled in Hazara in August, and in September his son Sher Singh's army joined the revolt. The Sikhs fought the British at Ramnagar in November and at Chillianwala in January 1849, but were decisively beaten at Gujrat on 21 February 1849. At the end of March 1849 the young Duleep Singh was deposed and the Punjab was annexed by the East India Company.
